Each premade's own encounter cards, dealt only to that traveler by a V10 journey started with personal roads (personalDeckV10.ts), and their own choices on shared cards, gated by their identity deed. Card art points at a reused gamebook scene until its painted plate ships (projects/zuzu-shifting-lands/art/ROUND-9-PERSONAL.yaml).

cards.title: A Straw Hat on the Current
cards.flavor: A wide straw hat comes turning down the river toward the landing, shallow-crowned and woven tight, the kind your own people wear on the road. Nobody here weaves them. The old otter who runs the ferry fishes it out with his pole and turns it over: the chin cord is knotted the way your teacher knotted his. He asks if it is yours. It is not. It cannot be.

choices.label: Ask where this river rises
choices.intent: Learn which water carried something from your country into this one.
choices.risk: Some questions open a door you cannot close.

success.text: The otter says the river rises nowhere: it comes up out of the dry ground past the Tablelands and sinks back into it at the Verge. Things from far away wash down it every spring, he says, and none of them ever go home. You keep the hat's cord, a little length of a knot you know.

failure.text: He shrugs and says a river is a river. You stand too long at the landing staring upstream, and the family waiting in the sun goes over without you. The next crossing is a long, hungry wait.

choices.label: Bow to it and let it go
choices.intent: Set the hat back on the water the way your people send off the dead.
choices.risk: You may never again see anything of home this close.

success.text: You take the hat from the ferryman, bow to it once, and set it back on the current. It turns twice and is gone. The otter takes off his own cap without being asked, and when you step aboard he will not take your fare.

choices.label: Buy the hat
choices.intent: Keep the only thing in this land that was made where you were made.
choices.risk: The ferryman can read how much you want it.

success.text: He names a price and you pay it without bargaining, which makes him look at you twice. The hat is damp and smells of a river you have never seen. You tie it to your pack, and at night it is the last thing you look at.

choices.label: Give it to the child in the sun
choices.intent: A family waits in the glare, and their smallest has no shade at all.
choices.risk: A piece of home goes on a stranger's head.

success.text: You take the hat from the ferryman and set it on the head of the smallest child waiting in the sun. It comes down past her ears. Her mother starts to refuse, sees your face, and stops. They cross under one patch of shade, and the child waves the brim at you from the far bank.

cards.title: The Smith Who Asks for Your Blade
cards.flavor: A pronghorn smith works a cart forge at the edge of the camp, mending wagon iron for food. She stops hammering when she sees the sword on your back and asks, very politely, to see the steel. Nobody here folds metal that way. A blade like that, she says, could become twenty plough points, and the camp is out of plough points. Behind her a family is trying to break dry ground with a stick.

choices.label: Show her how it was folded
choices.intent: Let her study the steel and learn the fold, and give her nothing else.
choices.risk: Showing a blade is close to drawing it.

success.text: You draw it slowly, edge away, and lay it across your sleeves. She looks for a long time and asks good questions. By morning she has folded a scrap of wagon spring the way you showed her, and it holds an edge. The family in the field has a real plough point by noon.

failure.text: Her hammer slips on the first fold and the scrap shatters across the anvil; a splinter opens your forearm. She apologizes over and over while she binds it. Your teacher spent a year on the fold, you remember, and still burned his hands.

choices.label: Give her the sword
choices.intent: Twenty plough points feed more mouths than one wanderer's sword ever will.
choices.risk: Where you come from, a sword is a soul. You would walk on without yours.

success.text: You unsling it, bow, and lay it in her hands. She does not understand what you have given and you do not explain. The camp eats from new furrows by spring. That night your back feels wrong and light, like a pack with nothing in it. You sleep anyway.

choices.label: Refuse with a bow
choices.intent: Keep the sword. Some things are not yours to trade.
choices.risk: The family in the field keeps its stick.

success.text: You bow and keep your hands still. The smith nods as if she expected nothing else and goes back to her wagon iron. Before you leave you help the family turn their field the slow way, with your own hands, until dark.

cards.title: Your Teacher's Voice in the Dark
cards.flavor: Where three tunnels meet, someone speaks your name in the language of home: not the name the road calls you, but the one your mother used. It is your teacher's voice, patient and dry. The way back is very short from here, it says, shorter than you would believe. It needs only one small thing from this side of the wall. The torches lean toward the voice as if it were breathing in.

choices.label: Ask what only he would know
choices.intent: Answer in your own tongue and test it with a question from his gate.
choices.risk: Talking to it at all is how it starts.

success.text: You ask the name of the tree outside his gate. The voice hesitates, then names a tree that never grew there. You bow to nothing and walk out of the crossroads with your hand on your hilt. Whatever it is, it does not know your home. It only knows you miss it.

failure.text: It answers correctly. It knows the tree, the gate, the crack in the third step. You stand listening much longer than you meant to, and when you come out your torch is a stub and your hands are cold to the wrist.

choices.label: Listen to the way home
choices.intent: Let it tell you the road, only to hear it said.
choices.risk: It wants one small thing from this side of the wall.

success.text: It tells you. The road is real and short, and at its end is the gate you left. It names the price gently, the way your teacher named pain: one small life from this side, a child nobody would miss. You do not agree. You do not forget it, either.

choices.label: Cover your ears and walk on
choices.intent: Take whichever tunnel the voice is not in.
choices.risk: Wrong tunnels run long down here.

success.text: You press your palms over your ears and walk until the voice is only the sound of water. The tunnel you chose opens at the cave mouth a little before dawn, with the stars spilled across the sky.

failure.text: You walk until the voice stops, and then until your legs do. The tunnel loops back on itself twice, and you eat the last of your dried fruit in the dark to keep going.

cards.title: Snow Through the Last Door
cards.flavor: At the last threshold one seam in the black rock is cold to the touch. Through it, impossibly, snow is falling on a curved wooden bridge, and past the bridge stands a gate you have walked through a thousand times. A bell is ringing there for the evening meal. Behind you the line of travelers waits at the threshold with their bundles and their children while the wardens count them.

choices.label: Step onto the bridge
choices.intent: Go home. You have earned it ten times over.
choices.risk: Something on the other side has been waiting for exactly this.

success.text: You step through. The snow is real, and the bridge creaks under you the way it always did. Halfway across you see that the bell at the gate has no clapper and is ringing anyway. You go back for your pack. You tell yourself it is only for your pack.

choices.label: Take off your hat and close it
choices.intent: Bow to home once, the way you bow to the dead, and push the seam shut.
choices.risk: There may never be another door.

success.text: You take off your hat, bow to the bridge and the gate and the evening bell, and lean your shoulder into the cold rock until the seam grinds shut. Snow melts on your sleeve. A child in the line is watching you, and does not ask why your face is wet.

failure.text: The seam will not close all the way. You leave it a finger wide, snow still sifting through, and the evening bell stays in your ears all night. You did not go. That will have to be enough.

choices.label: Watch it before anyone else goes
choices.intent: If it is a way out, the people in this line need it more than you do.
choices.risk: You do not know what waits on the far side for them.

success.text: You watch the far side long enough to see that the bell has no clapper and is ringing anyway. You put your back to the seam and turn the first family away from it, then the next. By the time the wardens notice, the seam has closed on its own. Nobody thanks you. Nobody went.

failure.text: You see nothing wrong, and an old badger steps through before you can decide. The seam closes behind him like a mouth. The whole line goes very quiet, and so do you.

cards.title: A Whistle From the Rocks
cards.flavor: Two notes, low then high, come from the rocks above the old well: the crew's call. You have not heard it since the dry well. A jackal kit you remember as all ears and elbows slides down the scree, thinner now, with a rag like yours tied round her arm. Hollis sent her. The crew is starving, she says, and Hollis wants her quartermaster back.

choices.label: Whistle back
choices.intent: Answer the call so they know you heard.
choices.risk: Answering is halfway to going.

success.text: You give the answer, high then low, and somewhere up in the rocks three more whistles answer you. The kit grins for the first time. She tells you where the crew is camped and which road they watch, and runs off to tell Hollis you are coming. You never said you were.

choices.label: Send food up the scree
choices.intent: Fill her arms with what you carry and send her back to the crew.
choices.risk: Two days of your food go to a band that robs wagons.

success.text: You empty your pack into her arms and add your spare boots on top. She looks at the boots longer than the food. "Hollis said you'd do that," she says, and is gone. That night a whistle sounds from the ridge twice, which in the crew means thank you, and also means we owe you.

choices.label: Ask about the little ones
choices.intent: Find out what became of the barefoot children you looked after.
choices.risk: You may not like the answer.

success.text: She tells you straight: the little ones left the crew when the water ran low, walking toward the canyons with the oldest girl in front. Two still had no boots. She points the way, and it is not the way the crew is camped.

failure.text: She shrugs and will not say, which tells you enough. You sit on the lip of the well a long time after she has gone, turning one small boot over and over in your paws.

choices.label: Tell her you're done with the crew
choices.intent: Say it out loud so you have to mean it.
choices.risk: Hollis don't take no from a scout.

success.text: "Tell Hollis I ain't coming," you say, and your voice only cracks once. The kit looks at you like you grew a foot. Nobody whistles from the rocks again, and you can't tell whether that is relief or the worst thing that has happened all week.

failure.text: You start to say it and it comes out sideways, a promise to think about it. The kit hears what you didn't say and runs to tell Hollis you're coming. Now you are expected.

cards.title: Hollis's Toll at the Seep
cards.flavor: The jackals of the dry well have come down to the delta, where one muddy seep still gives water, and they are charging travelers a cup of grain for a cup of water. Hollis sits on an overturned cart beside it with a rifle across her knees and her ribs showing through her coat. She sees your mask before she sees your face. "Mittens," she says. "Come to work, or come to drink?"

choices.label: Take your old post for a night
choices.intent: Scout for them again, just for tonight, to eat and to see.
choices.risk: You will be the one pointing at travelers' packs.

success.text: You sit on the rocks with the crew's spyglass and call out the wagons worth tolling, and for one night you eat like you have not eaten in a month. In the dark you count the crew's stores: almost nothing, and three kits hidden in the reeds. Hollis claps your shoulder. "Knew you'd come home."

failure.text: You point out a wagon and it turns out to be a family with nothing worth taking. The crew takes their last grain anyway. The youngest of them stares at you the whole time, and you cannot make yourself look away.

choices.label: Vouch for the poorest travelers
choices.intent: Ask Hollis to let the poorest drink free on your word.
choices.risk: Your word is worth what the crew thinks you owe them.

success.text: Hollis looks at you a long while, then at the line. "Your word," she says. "Any of 'em brings wardens, it's your neck." The poorest drink free till sundown and nobody brings wardens. Hollis doesn't thank you, but she lets you fill your canteen.

failure.text: "Your word," Hollis says, "ain't what it was." Two of the crew walk you away from the seep with your canteen still empty. Behind you the toll goes on, a cup for a cup.

choices.label: Tell her what you saw at Hollow Bell
choices.intent: Tell Hollis about the wax on the thresholds, and the beds emptied before the fire.
choices.risk: Some of her crew rode near Hollow Bell that week.

success.text: You tell her about the black wax and the empty beds. Hollis goes very still. Then she sends two of the crew south to watch the mission road, and halves the toll. "Anybody's taking kits," she says, "they come through us first."

failure.text: Hollis hears you out and laughs, not kindly. "Ghost stories," she says, "from a boy who strips boots." The crew laughs with her, and you leave the seep with hot ears and a story nobody would hear.

choices.label: Pay your cup and walk on
choices.intent: Pay like anyone else, drink, and leave without looking back.
choices.risk: Hollis does not like being treated like a stranger.

success.text: You pour a cup of grain into the bucket and drink a cup of brown water. Hollis watches you go and does not call after you, and neither does anybody else in the crew. It is what you wanted. It feels like being skinned.

cards.title: The Barefoot Line Grows
cards.flavor: In a dry adit at the edge of the quarry you find them: the barefoot children from Hollow Bell, or what is left of them, and more besides. There are nine now. The oldest girl has been doing your job, badly and bravely. She stands when she sees you and says, very formally, that the quartermaster is back, and every little one looks at the boots round your neck and then down at their own feet.

choices.label: Hand out every pair, smallest first
choices.intent: Empty the string and fit the smallest feet first.
choices.risk: You will have nothing left to trade on the road.

success.text: You kneel in the dust and fit them one by one, smallest first, lacing each pair the way your mother showed you. Four pairs for nine children; the rest get rag wraps and a promise. When you stand up your neck feels light and wrong and good.

choices.label: Lead them to Hollis's crew
choices.intent: The crew has water and rifles. The children have neither.
choices.risk: The crew has also learned to sell what it cannot feed.

success.text: You lead them down out of the quarry to the crew's fire, and Hollis takes them in without a word, which is better than you feared. The next morning the oldest girl is handed a spyglass and a post on the rocks. You know exactly what that means, because it is what it meant for you.

choices.label: Teach the oldest girl the job
choices.intent: Show her the gaps in the rocks, the water signs, and how to trade boots without getting caught.
choices.risk: Teaching her means planning to leave.

success.text: You spend the day teaching her everything: which water is safe, which wardens can be shamed, how to read a scout's whistle. By dark she is better at it than you were. She asks if you're leaving. You tell her the truth sideways, the way you always do, and she understands it anyway.

failure.text: She is too tired to learn, and you are too scared of what happens after you go to teach well. The day ends with nine hungry children and one plan, and it is a bad one.

choices.label: Stand watch over them tonight
choices.intent: Let them sleep for once without one eye open.
choices.risk: Nights in the quarry run cold and long.

success.text: You sit at the mouth of the adit all night with your little knife across your knees. Nobody comes. In the morning the smallest one says you snored, which is a lie, and the oldest girl says thank you, which isn't.

failure.text: Something does come near dawn: a coyote raider after the quarry's cistern. You chase him off with stones and shouting, and he catches you once with a stick before he goes. The children saw. They will remember that you stayed.

cards.title: The Crew Hired to Hold the Gate
cards.flavor: The wardens of the last threshold have hired guards to hold its gate against the refugees pressing at the fence, and the guards are Hollis's crew, fed for the first time in a year. Hollis spots your mask in the crowd outside. She sends the jackal kit to the fence with a message: there is a place for you inside, with food, if you come through now, alone.

choices.label: Go in alone
choices.intent: Take the place. Eat. Stop being hungry.
choices.risk: The crowd outside will see you go.

success.text: The gate opens a crack for you and closes behind. Inside there is stew, a blanket, and a post on the wall with a rifle you are almost tall enough to hold. From the wall you can see the crowd outside the fence, and the children in it. You eat anyway.

choices.label: Turn the crew
choices.intent: Get Hollis to open the gate from inside, for everyone.
choices.risk: The wardens are paying her, and they have more rifles.

success.text: You climb the fence and talk to Hollis through the stakes for an hour, about the dry well and the kits and Hollow Bell, until she stops arguing and starts thinking. At the change of watch the whole crew walks off their posts at once and the gate stands open. The wardens have nobody left to hold it.

failure.text: Hollis listens, and then she says no, gently, the way you would say it to a kit. "They feed us, Mittens." The gate stays shut. You climb down on the crowd's side and you stay there.

choices.label: Call in what Hollis owes you
choices.intent: She said once she would owe you. This is the time.
choices.risk: A favor called is a favor gone.

success.text: You send the kit back with one word: owed. A minute later the crew's whistle goes up, two notes, low then high, and the side gate swings open for the smallest children in the crowd. Hollis does not look at you. That is how she says you're square.

choices.label: Lead the crowd round by the rocks
choices.intent: You know every gap in these rocks. The gate is not the only way past.
choices.risk: The rocks are no place for the old and the small.

success.text: You find the gap the crew used to use and lead the crowd through it by twos and threes all night, carrying the smallest yourself. By dawn they are past the threshold and the wardens are guarding nothing. From the wall Hollis watches the line go, and does not raise her rifle.

failure.text: The gap has fallen in since the crew last used it. You get half the crowd through before the rocks shift, and you spend the rest of the night digging an old badger out with your paws. Everyone lives. Nobody else gets past.

cards.title: Warm Beds, Separate Rooms
cards.flavor: The sisters at the refuge are kind. They scrub Bao until he is fluffy and laughing, and offer you a dress with no holes in it, which you refuse. At bedtime the eldest sister explains, gently, that the little ones sleep in the warm room at the back and the big ones in the hall. Bao is already asleep on her shoulder. She has not asked you.

choices.label: Take him back
choices.intent: Lift him off her shoulder. He sleeps where you sleep.
choices.risk: The sisters do not like being refused twice in one evening.

success.text: You hold out your arms and wait until she has to hand him over or make a scene. She hands him over. You sleep in the hall with your back to the wall and Bao on your chest, and in the morning the sisters are polite and cold and do not offer breakfast.

choices.label: Let him go, and sleep across the door
choices.intent: Give him one warm night, and lie across the doorway of the warm room.
choices.risk: You will have to stay awake all night.

success.text: You lie across the threshold in your rags and pinch yourself awake every time your eyes close. Near midnight a sister comes down the hall with a candle, sees you, and goes back the way she came. Bao sleeps warm all night. In the morning you can barely stand, and you do not care.

failure.text: You fall asleep on the threshold. When you wake the door is open and his cot is empty, and your heart stops. You find him at the end of the hall in a sister's arms, being carried toward the chapel. You take him back screaming, the whole refuge wakes, and they let you both out into the dark because it is easier than explaining.

choices.label: Take the bread and go before dark
choices.intent: Eat what they give, fill your satchel, and be on the road by sundown.
choices.risk: A night on the road with a scrubbed, sleepy little brother.

success.text: You eat, fill your satchel while the sisters clear the plates, and are out the gate with Bao on your hip before the bedtime bell. You sleep in a ditch with the satchel for a pillow. It is the best night's sleep in a week, because you know exactly where he is.

failure.text: A sister catches you at the gate with your satchel full and takes back every crust, very kindly. She tells you the road is dangerous at night. You go anyway, hungry, with Bao heavy and warm on your hip.

choices.label: Let him sleep in the warm room
choices.intent: He is warm and fed and asleep. Let someone else carry him for one night.
choices.risk: You do not know why the little ones sleep apart.

success.text: You let the sister carry him away, lie down in the hall, and sleep like a stone for the first time since Hollow Bell. In the morning they bring him back scrubbed and quiet. He is very quiet. He will not talk about the warm room, and he will not let go of your sleeve all day.

cards.title: Half Fare for a Small One
cards.flavor: The ferryman charges full fare for a toddler, because, he says, a toddler is a passenger who can fall in. You have one ration left, and a school satchel you have carried since before the fire, with your name stitched inside the flap in your mother's thread. The water at the landing runs brown and fast. Bao is pointing at the boat and saying boat, boat, boat.

choices.label: Trade the satchel
choices.intent: The ferryman has been eyeing it. It is good leather.
choices.risk: It is the last thing you have from before.

success.text: You empty it into your arms and hand it over: a slate, a broken pencil, a ribbon, your stitched name. The ferryman takes it without knowing what it is. Bao rides the whole way across in the bow laughing at the spray, and you hold the slate and the ribbon and do not look back.

choices.label: Carry him across the ford
choices.intent: There is a ford upstream, waist-deep on a grown-up. You are not a grown-up.
choices.risk: Fast water, with him on your shoulders.

success.text: You lift him onto your shoulders, wade in where the water runs brown and fast, and cross one step at a time with your teeth clenched. Once it comes up to your chin. He thinks it is a game. On the far bank you sit in the mud and shake for a long time while he pats your ear.

failure.text: Halfway over the current takes your feet. You go under with him held up out of the water in both arms, and somehow come up on a gravel bar coughing brown water, with Bao still above you, screaming and alive. A fisherman pulls you both out. You do not remember the rest.

choices.label: Haggle like a grown-up
choices.intent: Stand on a crate and talk to him the way your mother talked to traders.
choices.risk: Ferrymen do not like being out-talked by a child.

success.text: You point out that a toddler on a hip takes no seat, that the boat is half empty, and that the next family will pay if they see him take you. He laughs at you and lets you both on for the one ration. Bao eats half of it anyway, from your hand, on the way across.

failure.text: He laughs and pushes off without you. You spend the afternoon on the bank while Bao cries, and when the boat comes back the ferryman lets you on for nothing, out of pity. Pity is worse.

choices.label: Stow away at dusk
choices.intent: Hide under the tarp on the last crossing.
choices.risk: A stowaway who is found gets put off midstream.

success.text: Under the tarp it smells of fish and wet rope, and you keep your hand over Bao's mouth every time he starts to say boat. Nobody finds you. You slip off on the far side in the dark. You feel clever for exactly one minute, and then you feel like a thief.

failure.text: Bao says boat at the worst possible moment. The ferryman drags back the tarp, says a word you are not allowed to say, then looks at the two of you and lets you stay. He makes you bail the whole way across.

cards.title: Fever by the Picket Fire
cards.flavor: Bao burns. It came on in the afternoon, and now he lies against you by the camp's picket fire with his huge ears hot and limp, too tired to cry. He has not eaten. He keeps his paw closed round the last crust you gave him, as if someone might take it. The camp healer charges, the trader has bark, and the night will be long.

choices.label: Give him your medicine
choices.intent: The medicine you have been carrying was always for this.
choices.risk: Then you will have none left.

success.text: You grind it between two stones and get it into him a little at a time, in water, while he fights you. By midnight he is sweating. By dawn he is cool, and hungry, and asking for apples. You did not sleep, and you do not need to.

choices.label: Sit up and keep him cool
choices.intent: Wet cloths and small sips all night, the way your mother did.
choices.risk: It might not be enough.

success.text: You sit up all night with a wet rag and a cup, singing the counting song from school under your breath. Near dawn the fever breaks on its own, the way they sometimes do. He opens his eyes and says your name, the first time he has ever said it right.

failure.text: The fever does not break. At first light you carry him through the camp asking anyone, everyone. A quarry widow gives you willow bark from her own pouch, and it works, slowly. You owe her something you can never pay back.

choices.label: Pay the trader's price
choices.intent: Give the trader whatever he asks for his bark.
choices.risk: He will ask for a lot.

success.text: He asks for nearly everything in your pack, and you give it, and he hands you a strip of bark the length of your finger. It is enough. By morning Bao is eating the trader's stew out of your bowl, because you have nothing else to put in it.

choices.label: Take a strip from the healer's jar
choices.intent: The healer's tent has a whole jar. She will not miss one strip.
choices.risk: If she does, the whole camp will know who.

success.text: You slip into the healer's tent while she sleeps, take one strip, only one, and are back at the fire before the guard turns. Bao's fever breaks by morning. The healer counts her jar and looks at you across the camp for a long moment, and says nothing at all.

failure.text: She is not asleep. She catches your wrist in the dark, looks at your face and then at the burning child by the fire, and gives you the strip. She also tells the whole camp in the morning, and nobody will share a fire with you after.

cards.title: The Voice Asks for the Small One
cards.flavor: At the cave mouth the dark smells of bread: fresh and warm, the kind your mother baked on feast days. A voice deep in the rock speaks in your mother's voice. There is a table down here, it says, where nobody is ever hungry, and a bed for each of you, and all it asks is that the small one come down first, by himself, so it can see him.

choices.label: Pick him up and run
choices.intent: Do not answer. Do not look back.
choices.risk: Running in the dark with him in your arms is how you fall.

success.text: You scoop him up before he can toddle toward the smell and run: out of the cave mouth, down the scree, all the way to the road, and you do not stop until the smell is gone. He thinks it was a game. You let him think so.

failure.text: You run and you fall hard on the scree, twisting so that he lands on you and not the rocks. Your knee is bleeding. Behind you the voice laughs in your mother's voice. You get up anyway, and you keep running.

choices.label: Answer it in her words
choices.intent: Tell it what your mother would have told it.
choices.risk: It knows her voice better than you do now.

success.text: You tell it what she used to say at the door to traders: we feed ourselves, thank you, and you can keep your bread. The smell goes stale at once, like a loaf left out for a week, and the voice stops. Bao claps. You walk out holding his hand, and your own hand is shaking, and you do not let him see.

failure.text: You open your mouth and only your own voice comes out, small and scared. The dark waits, patient. You back out of the cave step by step with Bao clutched against you, and the smell of bread follows you halfway to the road.

choices.label: Go down and see the table
choices.intent: Only to look. You will carry him the whole way and never let go.
choices.risk: It asked for him to come alone. It never said it would not take him another way.

success.text: You carry him down a long way, and there is a table, and there is bread, and you both eat, and it is the best thing you have ever tasted. When you climb out the sun is in the wrong place and three days of road have gone by without you. Bao is fine. Bao is fine. He keeps asking when you are going back.

choices.label: Cover his ears and sing
choices.intent: Sing the counting song loud enough that he hears you and not it.
choices.risk: You will be singing alone at a cave mouth in the dark.

success.text: You press his big ears flat and sing the counting song loud and badly, all the way to a hundred and back. By the time you finish the smell is gone, Bao is asleep, and the cave is only a cave.

failure.text: You get to forty and lose the numbers. In the quiet the voice says his name, gently, and he wriggles toward it. You hold on so hard he cries, and carry him away still crying, and he does not forgive you until supper.

cards.title: A Year of Water on Your Head
cards.flavor: Your face is nailed above the trading post counter, drawn from the wrong side so the patch sits over the wrong eye. A year of water from the Dustwater water house, it says, to whoever brings you in. A thin opossum with three kits at his heels reads it twice, then looks at you, then at the kits' cracked lips. He has not decided yet. Neither have you.

choices.label: Let him bring you in
choices.intent: Walk to the water house with him, let him draw his year of water, and be gone before the guards wake.
choices.risk: The water house lockup has held better than you.

success.text: You walk in ahead of him with your paws where the clerk can see them. He gets his tin ticket for a year, and his kits drink at the trough while you are led downstairs. At midnight you work the window bar loose with a spoon you palmed at supper and go over the back wall. Behind you, a family has water till next summer.

failure.text: He gets his ticket. You get the lockup, and the bar does not give until the second night, when a guard catches you halfway through the window and takes his pay out of your ribs. You go over the wall anyway. The kits, at least, are drinking.

choices.label: Let him see the gun
choices.intent: Open your coat a hand's width and let him do the sums.
choices.risk: A father with three thirsty kits may not do sums the way you would.

success.text: He looks at the gun, then at his kits, and does the sums. He buys a half sack of meal and goes out without looking at the wall again. The trader sells you jerky and says nothing. It is the way the world used to work for you, and it still works.

failure.text: He looks at the gun and goes for the trader's rifle behind the counter anyway. You are out the back door before he gets it up, with a fresh hole in the door frame beside your ear and no supplies. Behind you a kit starts to cry.

choices.label: Tell him what that water costs
choices.intent: Tell him about the night wagons you drove from the water house to the mission gate.
choices.risk: A wanted coyote's story is worth less than a year of water.

success.text: You tell it plainly: the wagons with the canvas tied down, the gate, the night you finally looked. He listens with one paw on his oldest kit's head. When you finish he takes the notice off the nail himself, folds it small, and gives it to the kit to start their supper fire.

failure.text: He hears you out with his jaw set, and you watch him decide you are a liar with a good tongue. He goes to tell the water house where you are. You leave Dustwater by the dry wash before dark, with less food than you came in with.

choices.label: Buy his kits a jug and go
choices.intent: Trade your own food for their water and leave before he finishes deciding.
choices.risk: Kindness from a wanted face looks a lot like a bribe.

success.text: You put two days of food on the counter and point at the kits. The trader fills a jug. The opossum takes it without a word, and you are out the door before he works out whether he was paid to forget your face. Maybe he was.

cards.title: The Gate You Drove Up To
cards.flavor: You know this gate. You have seen it twice before from the seat of a water house wagon, with the canvas tied down behind you and orders not to look under it. The same young sister in grey opens it now, lamp in hand, and smiles as if you were expected. "You've come without the wagon," she says. "Mother will be sorry. She asked after you."

choices.label: Ask to see the ones you brought
choices.intent: Ask after the children from your two wagons, by the count if not by name.
choices.risk: You may get an answer.

success.text: She walks you through a long dormitory where every bed is made tight and every bed is empty. They have gone on to the far house, she says, and she cannot give you its road. She is lying, and lying well, and you know the look: you wore it on the wagon seat all last year.

failure.text: They are sleeping, she says, and it would be unkind to wake them. The gate closes on you gently. You stand in the road until the lamp in the window goes out, and you never do learn how many beds were full.

choices.label: Sit at the bend and turn families back
choices.intent: Spend the day below the gate warning anyone who comes up the road with children.
choices.risk: Nobody listens to a one-eyed drifter with a price on his head.

success.text: You sit on a rock at the bend all day with your hat in your paws. Most families walk past you. Two stop, hear you out, look up at the gate, and turn their wagons round. One mother leaves a heel of bread on the rock beside you without saying why.

failure.text: A father with a pitchfork runs you off the bend before noon, sure you are a road agent waiting for his cart. From the ridge you watch him drive his little ones up to the gate, and the sister in grey comes out smiling to meet them.

choices.label: Take the supper she offers
choices.intent: You are hungry, and the soup smells like soup.
choices.risk: Nothing in this place is free. You of all travelers know that.

success.text: The soup is hot and the bread is soft and you eat until you are ashamed. They give you a clean cot in a room that locks from the outside. In the morning the door stands open, your boots are polished, and the guest ledger has a fresh line in it describing you. You leave fast.

cards.title: Runaways at the Canyon Fire
cards.flavor: Seven travelers share one fire at the canyon camp, and two of them are children too careful for their age: a lynx girl and her small brother with no grown-up of their own. Across the flames a tall rider in a water house coat warms his paws. He knows your face. He says quietly that the water house would burn your notice for two strays who ran from a mission wagon, and he does not look at the children, which is how you know he means them.

choices.label: Take his trade
choices.intent: Two strays for your name off every post in Dustwater.
choices.risk: You have driven this road before. You know where it ends.

success.text: You do not have to touch them. You only nod. In the morning the rider walks them to his wagon with a paw on each small shoulder, and drops your notice into the coals as he goes. The girl looks back once. You are a free coyote now, free as anybody on the road, and you have never carried anything so heavy.

choices.label: Sit up between them and the coat
choices.intent: Put your back to the children and your gun on your knee, and stay awake.
choices.risk: He has all night, and you are tired.

success.text: You sit up all night between the children and the coat, gun on your knee, and you do not blink first. Before dawn the rider saddles up and goes without a word. The girl leaves half her bread by your boot and will not look at you while you eat it.

failure.text: You doze once near dawn and wake to his paw on the girl's sleeve. You get between them, and he lays his rifle butt across your head for it, but the camp is awake now and he rides out alone. The children stay by the fire. So do you, with your head ringing.

choices.label: Walk them out by the side canyon
choices.intent: Wake them quietly and lead them up a side canyon to freighters going the other way.
choices.risk: Side canyons at night are no place for small feet.

success.text: You carry the boy and the girl carries your hat, and by moonrise you are over the rim and down at a freighters' camp bound north, away from every wagon road you know. A mule driver's wife takes one look and makes room by her fire. You walk back alone before the rider wakes.

failure.text: The side canyon pinches shut in the dark, and you spend half the night finding another way down with the boy asleep on your shoulder. You reach the freighters at dawn, footsore and scraped, with the rider's tracks already on the trail behind. The children are safe. You are not rested.

choices.label: Tell the fire what his coat means
choices.intent: Say out loud, to all seven, what the water house rider is here for.
choices.risk: Some of them may want a year of water too.

success.text: You say it plain: water house coat, mission wagons, two children with no grown-up. The fire goes quiet. Then an old ewe moves to sit beside the lynx girl, and a ferret beside the boy, and the rider finds himself alone on his side of the flames. He leaves at first light.

failure.text: Nobody at the fire believes a wanted coyote over a coat with brass buttons. The rider smiles and offers round his canteen. You take the children out of camp yourself before dawn, with nothing for the road but what you carry.

cards.title: The Wagon on the Glass
cards.flavor: A covered wagon creaks along the black glass ahead of you with its canvas tied down tight, the way you used to tie it. The driver is a young ferret in a coat too good for him, and he keeps his eyes on the road the way you were told to keep yours. Something small knocks twice on the boards from inside. Your paw is on your gun before you have decided anything.

choices.label: Step into the road and stop it
choices.intent: Do what you did once on the Dustwater road, and cut the canvas.
choices.risk: A scared driver with a whip can run a coyote down.

success.text: You step into the road with your gun out, and the driver hauls up, because once you would have too. You cut the ties. Four children blink up at the glare, thirsty and frightened and whole. You give them your water, point them at the threshold camp, and send the driver walking back the way he came.

failure.text: He lays on the whip and the mules lunge, and you have to run the black glass to catch the brake. You go down hard and skin both palms on the stones, but the brake holds and the wagon stops. When you cut the canvas, four children stare out at you, whole. Your paws will heal.

choices.label: Climb up and lay your gun on the seat
choices.intent: Sit beside him, set the gun between you, and talk the way nobody talked to you.
choices.risk: A frightened boy beside a loaded gun.

success.text: You tell him about the gate, the made beds, the year you drove. He drives a mile without a word. Then he turns the mules off the road toward the threshold camp and unties the canvas himself. When he climbs down he asks to keep the gun, so nobody can make him drive again. You let him.

failure.text: He snatches the gun and points it at your chest with both paws shaking. You talk slow for a long time. In the end he throws it into the ash and runs, and you drive the wagon to the threshold camp yourself, unarmed for the first time in eleven years.

choices.label: Let it go by
choices.intent: It is not your wagon. Not this time.
choices.risk: You will hear that knocking for a while.

success.text: The wagon creaks on toward the dark country. The knocking stops after a while, or you get too far away to hear it. You tell yourself that is the same thing, and you keep walking, and you keep telling yourself.

cards.title: The Fever Wagon at the Post
cards.flavor: A covered wagon waits outside the trading post with a little bell burned into its tailboard: the same wagon, or its twin, that carried your boy up the mission road. A young mother stands beside it with a kit hot with fever wrapped against her chest. The driver is kind about it. The good sisters will have the child well by spring, he says. Your paw is on the scattergun before you have decided anything.

choices.label: Tell her about Lark
choices.intent: Tell her plainly where your boy went, and that he never came back.
choices.risk: The truth is cruel, and she has nothing else to try.

success.text: You tell her about the fever, and the wagon, and how kind they were about it, and how no letter ever came. She does not want to hear it. Then she looks at the bell burned into the tailboard and pulls the blanket tighter round her kit. The wagon goes up the mission road without them.

failure.text: She hears a grieving barkeep with a gun, and that is all she hears. "Yours was different," she says, and climbs aboard. You stand in the dust until the wagon is a smudge on the mission road, saying his name under your breath.

choices.label: Buy fever bark for the kit
choices.intent: Spend your road food on bark, so she has a reason to stay.
choices.risk: Bark is dear in Dustwater, and it may not be enough.

success.text: You trade two days of food for a twist of willow bark and show her how to steep it, the way you should have done yourself that spring. The kit sweats through the night on a bench inside the post. By morning the fever has broken, and the wagon has gone on without them.

choices.label: Hold the wagon at gunpoint
choices.intent: Put both barrels on the driver until the mother changes her mind.
choices.risk: The post is full of folk who drink the water that wagon pays for.

success.text: You step into the road with the scattergun level and tell the driver he is going nowhere today. He goes white and stays put. The mother backs into the post with her kit, and by the time the trader fetches the wardens the wagon has turned round empty. They write your name in a book.

failure.text: The driver flicks the reins and the mules lunge, and you don't fire. You never could fire at a wagon. The wardens take your shells and leave you the gun, and the whole post watches the wagon go up the road with the mother aboard.

choices.label: Let her go with her hope
choices.intent: Say nothing. You were let hope once.
choices.risk: You know exactly what silence costs.

success.text: You say nothing, the way the whole town said nothing to you. The mother climbs up with her kit and thanks the driver for his kindness. You go inside and order a drink you don't drink, at a bar that isn't yours, and watch the road through the window until dark.

cards.title: Torches at the Refuge Wall
cards.flavor: Word has gone round the refuge yard that a drover's kit vanished from the bunkroom in the night, and the sisters say she went home. The travelers gather by the woodpile with lamp oil and hard faces, and they keep looking at you: the Dustwater barkeep with the scattergun and the boy on a notice. One of them holds out a torch, already lit. "You know what they are," he says. "Say the word."

choices.label: Say the word
choices.intent: Lead them to the back wing with fire, the way you have dreamed of every night since spring.
choices.risk: Fire does not choose.

success.text: You say it, and they follow you. The back wing goes up like dry grass. The sisters carry the little ones out through the kitchen, every one, coughing in their nightclothes, and the travelers who slept here will sleep on the road tomorrow. You do not find Lark, or the drover's kit. The old sister who tends the lantern looks at you across the yard as if you are the thing she was afraid of.

choices.label: Stand them down
choices.intent: Get between the torches and the wall and talk them out of it.
choices.risk: They came to you because they want the fire.

success.text: You put yourself between the woodpile and the wall and say what nobody said to you: that fire does not choose, that a burned house tells nobody anything, and that tomorrow they will want to know. One by one the torches go into the water trough. In the morning three of them walk with you to ask questions in daylight.

failure.text: They hear you out and shoulder past. You spend the night running buckets with the sisters, and the wing is saved by a wet wind and nothing else. Nobody thanks you, on either side of the wall.

choices.label: Search the back wing yourself
choices.intent: Go in with a lamp before anyone goes in with a torch.
choices.risk: The sisters will not want you there, and they will remember.

success.text: You go round by the woodshed and in through the scullery. The bunkroom is stripped. Under the last cot, scratched into the floorboard where a small paw could reach, is a name that is not Lark's, and beside it a row of tally marks. You copy every mark onto the back of his notice and come out with something better than fire: proof.

failure.text: A sister meets you at the scullery door with a lamp of her own and a smile like a closed gate. "Lost, dear?" She walks you back to the yard herself. By morning the bunkroom is scrubbed, and the travelers' torches have gone out on their own.

choices.label: Leave before first light
choices.intent: Take your gun and go, before they light anything with your name on it.
choices.risk: Whatever happens here happens without you.

success.text: You fill your canteen at the trough and walk out of the gate in the dark. From the first rise you look back and see no fire, and you never learn whether that is because you left, or in spite of it.

cards.title: The Teamster Who Drove the Wagon
cards.flavor: At the canyon camp a young mule-teamster shares your fire, sees the notice folded in your hatband, and goes grey under his dust. He drove for Vane two summers, he says. He remembers a rabbit boy with a bent ear who sang the whole way up the mission road to keep from crying. He has not slept right since. He holds his empty cup out to you like a kit holding out something broken.

choices.label: Fill his cup and let him talk
choices.intent: Truth for kindness: the bargain you kept behind the bar for twenty years.
choices.risk: You will hear all of it.

success.text: You fill his cup from your flask and say nothing until he has said everything: the song, the gate, the sister who lifted your boy down and called him by name, and the stair door he saw shut behind them. When he is done he is shaking and you are not. Now you know where to go. You give him the rest of the flask.

failure.text: He gets as far as the gate and stops, and will not say more however long you wait. In the morning he is gone before light. He has left his cup by your bedroll, filled with water, the way you would set one on a bar.

choices.label: Put both barrels on him
choices.intent: He drove your boy to that house. Make him answer for it here.
choices.risk: A camp full of strangers is watching.

success.text: You have the scattergun under his chin before the camp sees you move. He doesn't beg. He tells you everything, fast, and then he just waits. In the end you lower the gun, and he walks out of the firelight, and nobody at the camp will sit near you again.

failure.text: Two drovers take the gun off you before you can decide what you meant by it. The teamster is gone by morning. So are your shells, and the camp's welcome.

choices.label: Tell him you forgive him
choices.intent: Say it whether you mean it or not, so one of you can sleep.
choices.risk: You are not sure it is yours to give.

success.text: "You were hired to drive," you say. "I was the one lifted him up onto that wagon." It is the first time you have said it out loud. He cries like a kit. You don't. In the morning he is gone, and on your bedroll he has left a wagon pass with Vane's seal on it, the mission road's mile-marks drawn on the back.

failure.text: You try to say it, and the words come out as his name and yours and Lark's, all in the wrong order. He nods as if he understood. Maybe he did. You both sit by the fire until it is out, and neither of you sleeps.

choices.label: Tell the whole camp what he did
choices.intent: Let every fire in the canyon know what Vane's teamsters carry.
choices.risk: The camp will not stop at words.

success.text: You stand and tell it to the whole camp. By the time you sit down nobody will share a pot with him, and two drovers have taken his mules for what Vane owes them. He walks out of the canyon on foot at dawn. It feels like justice for almost an hour.

cards.title: A Bent Ear in the Gate Line
cards.flavor: In the crowd pressing at the last gate there is a rabbit boy of about seven with one ear bent over, alone, holding a wardens' tag he cannot read. He is not Lark. Lark would be grown by now, or would be nothing at all. Your heart does not care. The wardens are passing families through and turning back children who have nobody to vouch for them.

choices.label: Tell the wardens he's yours
choices.intent: Lie to the gate with your whole face.
choices.risk: Wardens know a lie when it is that hungry.

success.text: "Mine," you say, and put your paw on his head, and the warden looks from your ears to his and waves you both through. On the far side he asks your name. You tell him. He tells you his, and it is not Lark, and you find you can bear that.

failure.text: The warden asks the boy his mother's name, and he gives one that is not yours. They send you both to the back of the line. He stays beside you anyway, holding your coat, and you wait out the night together.

choices.label: Ask him his name
choices.intent: Before anything else, find out who he is.
choices.risk: You might not want to know.

success.text: His name is Bramble. His mother is two places ahead in the line, asleep on her feet, and he wandered back to look at your gun. You walk him to her and stand there while she wakes and grabs him. Then you take Lark's notice out of your hatband and put it away inside your coat, where it is warm.

failure.text: He won't say. He looks at your scattergun and then at your ears. You stand beside him until a warden calls a family name and a woman shouts it back, and he runs to her. He does not look round. He does not owe you that.

choices.label: Hand the wardens your scattergun
choices.intent: They want weapons left at the gate. Give them yours, and the shells, and whatever you meant to do with them.
choices.risk: You have not been without it since the spring he went.

success.text: You lay the scattergun on the wardens' table with both shells beside it, and walk toward the gate with empty paws. They feel strange. Behind you the boy with the bent ear is lifted up by someone who knows his name.

choices.label: Push to the front alone
choices.intent: You came to cross. Cross.
choices.risk: He will watch you go.

success.text: You shoulder through to the gate and show your papers and go through. When you look back, the boy with the bent ear is still holding his tag, still alone, and the wardens are already turning to the next family.

cards.title: The Chalk on the Gatepost
cards.flavor: Two seasons back, before the dry well gave out, you chalked the band's sign on this gatepost: full cellar, old ewe alone, no dogs. The chalk is still there. So is the ewe, leaning on a crutch in her doorway, watching your band come up the lane thin as rakes. Above the road, in the rocks, your three kits are keeping still the way you taught them.

choices.label: Take the cellar, as you planned it
choices.intent: Walk the band in and empty the root cellar while she watches.
choices.risk: She will know your face, and so will every farm she talks to.

success.text: Nobody has to raise a rifle. The ewe stands aside on her crutch and says nothing while the band carries out sacks of potatoes and a crock of lard. The kits eat that night till their bellies are tight as drums. In the morning the chalk is still on the post, and it means something different now.

choices.label: Offer the band's backs for a share
choices.intent: Dig her potatoes and mend her fence for a fair cut of the crop.
choices.risk: A raider band that digs is a raider band standing still where wardens can find it.

success.text: The band grumbles, then digs. By dark there are forty sacks in her cellar and six on your cart, and the ewe sends a jar of plum preserve up into the rocks without being asked. She knew all along the kits were there. "Kits shouldn't hide from a farm," she says.

failure.text: Half the band digs till noon, then walks off to sit in the shade and argue. You finish the row alone. The ewe pays you for the row and no more, and she is right to.

choices.label: Scrub the chalk off and walk on
choices.intent: Rub the mark out with your sleeve so no other band reads it, and lead your hungry crew past.
choices.risk: The band will go to sleep hungry, and they will know why.

success.text: You rub the chalk out with your sleeve while the band watches from the lane. Nobody says a word, which is worse than an argument. That night the kits split one heel of bread four ways, and the oldest gives you the biggest piece without being asked.

choices.label: Tell her who chalked her gate
choices.intent: She ought to know what the mark means, and who made it.
choices.risk: An old ewe on a crutch can still send for wardens.

success.text: She hears you out, leaning on the crutch. Then she spits on her paw and finishes rubbing the mark out herself. "Fed four of my own through a drought," she says, "and robbed a farm to do it." She gives you seed potatoes, not eating ones. They will be food next year, if you stop anywhere long enough.

failure.text: She hears you out, then shuts her door and bars it. Before the band is out of the lane a boy on a mule is riding hard for the wardens' post. You bring the kits down out of the rocks in the dark and keep moving.

cards.title: The Rifle on the Counter
cards.flavor: The trader sells flour to anyone with coin, and your band has no coin. What it has is the rifle: the one that lay across your knees every day at the dry well, the one the whole crew counts on without saying so. The trader has already seen it. He names a price in flour that would carry the kits to the canyons, and waits, polishing a cup that does not need it.

choices.label: Lay the rifle on the counter
choices.intent: Trade the crew's last gun for flour and walk out with nothing to raid with.
choices.risk: A band without a gun is just a hungry family on a road.

success.text: You set it on the counter and take your paws away before they change their mind. The trader weighs the flour fair. Outside, the crew looks at your empty shoulder and nobody speaks for a mile. Then your oldest kit takes your paw, which she has not done since she was small.

choices.label: Come back at closing
choices.intent: Keep the rifle and put it to the trader's back door after dark.
choices.risk: A post this size keeps a watchman, and a watchman keeps a bell.

success.text: You and two of the crew come in the back at closing, and the trader hands over flour and a tin of coffee without a fight. He looks at you the whole time, memorizing. By morning the band is twenty miles on and fed, and your face is in a stranger's head for good.

failure.text: The watchman rings the bell before you are through the door. The crew scatters into the dark with nothing, and a shot goes past close enough that you feel the air move. Your face will be on a notice by noon.

choices.label: Hire the band out as freight guards
choices.intent: Keep the gun and put it to honest work riding with a widow's salt wagons.
choices.risk: Every wagon road out of here runs past bands like yours, and they know your ear.

success.text: The salt widow looks your crew over and asks only whether they can count. Three days riding her wagons to the river and nobody tries them, because everybody on that road knows whose band it is. She pays in flour, and in a letter that says you kept her load whole.

failure.text: The widow says no, politely, and the next freight master says it less politely. Word of the dry well band got here ahead of you. You leave with the rifle and an empty flour sack.

choices.label: Pawn the rifle on your word
choices.intent: Leave it in his keeping against the flour, and swear to come back for it.
choices.risk: A word you cannot keep is worse than a gun you sold.

success.text: The trader has heard you keep your word, even raiding. He writes the pawn in his book and hangs the rifle on the wall behind him, where the crew can see it through the window. You walk out with flour and a debt you mean to pay, and the band walks out without a gun.

cards.title: The Caravan at the Fire
cards.flavor: There is one place left at the canyon camp's fire, and the family across it are mule drivers off the salt road. Last spring your band stopped their caravan at the dry well and took everything but the mules. The father knows your notched ear before he knows your face. He does not get up. He puts a paw on his little girl's shoulder and says to the whole fire, quietly, "That's her."

choices.label: Own it and pay what you can
choices.intent: Say yes, it was you, and set what the band carries at his feet.
choices.risk: It will not cover a quarter of what you took.

success.text: "It was me," you say, and set your sacks down by his boots. It is not enough, and everybody at the fire knows it. He keeps the sacks. Later, when the fire is low, he passes his girl's bowl round to your kits, and nobody at that camp says a word about it, then or ever.

choices.label: Tell him he has the wrong jackal
choices.intent: Plenty of jackals have notched ears. Keep your seat by the fire.
choices.risk: Lies told in front of kits get learned.

success.text: You laugh, easy, and say the salt road is thick with jackals. The fire decides to believe you, because believing you is less trouble. You keep your seat. Your oldest kit watches you across the flames all night, and in the morning she does not take your paw.

failure.text: Your oldest kit says "Mama?" out loud, surprised, before she can stop herself. The camp puts your band out on the cold side of the canyon with no fire, and you spend the night with all three kits buttoned inside your coat.

choices.label: Stand the camp's whole night watch
choices.intent: Put your band on the rim all night so the camp sleeps, his family with it.
choices.risk: A raider band on the rim in the dark looks exactly like what it is.

success.text: You put the crew on the rim in pairs and walk the line yourself till dawn. Near midnight something comes up the wash, a gang with no fire, and turns back when your band whistles. At breakfast the mule driver brings you a cup of coffee. He does not say anything, and does not need to.

failure.text: Nothing comes, and you are glad of it, but the camp sleeps badly with your band on the rim, and half of them sit up all night with their own guns. In the morning the mule driver tells you he counted his mules twice. Still, he counted them all.

cards.title: The Captain's Contract
cards.flavor: The warden captain of the fortified camp watched your band come in, and he knows a fighting crew when he sees one. He offers you a paper. Every mouth in the band fed, kits included, a roof inside the stockade, and coin besides. All you have to do is hold the threshold gate against the refugees massing on the road behind you. He lays a pen on the paper and turns it to face you.

choices.label: Sign the captain's paper
choices.intent: Feed the kits. Hold the gate. Do the sum every mother does.
choices.risk: Most of the refugees on that road are mothers too.

success.text: You sign. That night your kits sleep under a roof with full bellies for the first time since the dry well. In the morning you take the band up on the wall, and from there you can see the road, and the families on it, and their children. You count your own instead. Three. You keep counting.

choices.label: Tell him no to his face
choices.intent: Push the paper back across the table and tell him why.
choices.risk: Captains do not like raiders telling them what is decent.

success.text: "We been on that road," you say, and push the paper back. The captain studies you a long while and then, to your surprise, laughs. He lets the band sleep against the outside of the stockade where it is out of the wind, and he does not ask again.

failure.text: The captain hears you out and has the band put back on the road by dark, among the very families you would not hold off. A sentry's rifle butt catches you going through the gate. The families on the road make room for your kits anyway.

choices.label: Take the advance and walk off at night
choices.intent: Sign, eat, draw a week's flour ahead, and be gone before first watch.
choices.risk: A captain cheated is a captain with a long memory and a great many riders.

success.text: You sign with a flourish, draw the week's flour, and walk the band out through the rocks at the change of watch. By dawn you are miles off with full sacks, and the captain is short a gate crew. It is the best raid you ever pulled, and nobody bled for it.

failure.text: The sentries are better than their captain. They catch the band at the rocks with the flour on your backs and take it back, and a good deal more besides. You are put out on the road marked as a thief, which, tonight, you are.

choices.label: Ask what became of the last crew he hired
choices.intent: Somebody held that gate before you. Find out where they are now.
choices.risk: He may not like the question, and you may not like the answer.

success.text: The camp cook tells you what the captain will not. The last crew held the gate one winter and were put out with the refugees in spring, when the coin ran short. They are out on that road now, somewhere in the crowd. You fold the paper small and keep it in your coat, to remember by.

failure.text: Nobody will tell you, which is its own answer. The pen stays where the captain laid it, the paper stays on the table, and your kits are still hungry outside the stockade.

cards.title: Two Sisters at the Windlass
cards.flavor: Two sisters from the convent have come down to the old well with a mule and a water cart, and they are asking the well folk, very kindly, whether anyone has seen a runaway novice. One is Sister Teasel, who taught you your letters. The other is a novice younger than you, with her paws in her sleeves. You are crouched behind the trough with your habit rolled in a sack and the stair key still warm against your ribs.

choices.label: Drop a word in their bucket
choices.intent: Write GO on a scrap and float it where the young novice will draw it up.
choices.risk: Sister Teasel draws water too.

success.text: You fold the scrap small and drop it while Sister Teasel is busy asking the well folk about you. The young novice draws the bucket, and her paw goes into the water and out again, quick, the way yours did once. She does not look toward the trough. That night, from the ridge, you watch a small figure leave the cart and walk east.

failure.text: Sister Teasel draws the bucket herself, reads the scrap, and folds it into her sleeve. "Poor Wren," she tells the well folk, fondly. "She has always had nightmares." The well folk nod. The young novice rides home on the cart with Sister Teasel's paw resting on her shoulder the whole way.

choices.label: Step out and say why you ran
choices.intent: Say it in the open, in front of the habit you ran from.
choices.risk: The well folk have known those sisters for years. They have known you a minute.

success.text: You stand up from behind the trough and tell them about the stair door and the beds stripped to the boards. Your voice shakes the whole time. Sister Teasel says nothing at all, which is worse for her than anything she could have said. The well folk do not drive the sisters off, but they do not give them a drop of water either, and the cart goes home dry.

failure.text: Sister Teasel lets you finish, then says your name the way they always said it, like calling a dog that strays. The well folk look at her habit and at your sack and make up their minds. You run before anyone lays a paw on you, and you leave your water skin behind.

choices.label: Go down into the well
choices.intent: Otters hold a breath a long time. Sisters cannot see under water.
choices.risk: The shaft is deep, the water is cold, and they will draw a lot of buckets.

success.text: You slip over the rim and down the rope and hang under the black water while the buckets come down past you, four, five, six. When the cart has gone you climb out blue and shaking, and an old well keeper wraps you in a horse blanket and asks no questions at all. The young novice went home with them. You were safe. You sit with both of those a long time.

failure.text: The cold gets into your chest before the sixth bucket, and you come up coughing. Sister Teasel only sighs and says you'll catch your death, and then they leave you there. It is the kindest thing they have ever done for you, and it frightens you more than the stair.

cards.title: The Sister House Barge
cards.flavor: A flat barge with a little bell burned into its bow is loading at the landing for the sister house downriver. Two small children sit on its deck with paper tags pinned to their coats. Sister Agnete, who kept the keys when you were small, sees you on the dock and comes ashore smiling. All is forgiven, she says. You may even go your own way. She only needs to know where the rabbit kit who ran with you is hiding.

choices.label: Tell her where the kit is
choices.intent: Buy your own freedom with one small name.
choices.risk: You will know where that barge went for the rest of your life.

success.text: You tell her: the ferry cook's loft, behind the net barrels. Sister Agnete pats your cheek and thanks you, and she keeps her word. Nobody follows you up the bank. At dusk the barge casts off with three tags on its deck instead of two, and you stand on the landing and watch it until the river bends.

choices.label: Swim the children off at dusk
choices.intent: You were an otter before you were a novice. Go under the barge and come up on the river side.
choices.risk: The current is fast, and the children cannot swim.

success.text: At dusk you slip off the end of the dock and go under the barge's flat bottom and come up on the river side, where nobody is looking. You unpin the tags and let the river have them, and carry the children one at a time on your back to the reeds. Sister Agnete is still searching the ferry cook's loft when you are a mile downstream.

failure.text: You get the first child ashore in the reeds. When you go back for the second, there is a lantern on the stern and a sister watching the water. You lie in the shallows till your teeth chatter, and the barge casts off with one small passenger instead of two.

choices.label: Tell her the kit drowned
choices.intent: A lie told in a habit's voice. You learned from the best.
choices.risk: Sister Agnete taught you how to tell when a novice is lying.

success.text: You look at the river and let your eyes fill, and say the crossing was too fast for her. Sister Agnete makes the sign over the water, kindly, and goes back to her barge. The lie sits in your mouth like a stone all the way to the ferry cook's loft, where a small rabbit is waiting for you.

failure.text: Sister Agnete listens with her head on one side, the way she used to at confession. "Wren," she says gently. "You never could." She sends two drovers along the landing. You and the kit go out the back of the loft and into the reeds with nothing but what you are wearing.

choices.label: Walk away up the bank
choices.intent: Refuse her and go, and take nothing and no one.
choices.risk: The two on the deck are not yours to save, you tell yourself.

success.text: You tell Sister Agnete no, and walk up the bank without looking back, and she lets you. Your heart is going like a bird's. Behind you the barge casts off with its two small passengers, and you are halfway to the reeds before you let yourself think that you could have tried.

cards.title: A Draft That Smells of Wax
cards.flavor: At the crossroads one passage goes down: a cut stair, worn smooth in the middle, breathing up a warm draft that smells of candle wax and new bread. You know that smell. It came up under the cellar door every night you lay counting beds. Someone has chalked a child's arrow on the wall, pointing down. The iron key at your belt, the one you never gave back, has gone warm.

choices.label: Try the convent key in the gate
choices.intent: There is an old iron gate across the stair. Your key has opened one stair door already.
choices.risk: Some locks are made to be opened from below.

success.text: The key fits. Of course it fits. You swing the rusted gate shut and turn the key until the bolt goes home, and then you snap the bow off in the lock so nobody can turn it back, from either side. The draft stops. Your paws do not shake at all until you are a long way off.

failure.text: The key turns and turns and catches nothing. From far below, under the draft, someone says your name kindly, the way the Abbess said it. You run, and you do not stop until the wax smell is gone and your knees are skinned from the dark.

choices.label: Rub out the arrow and chalk one pointing up
choices.intent: Whoever drew it was small. The next small one should go the other way.
choices.risk: Whoever drew the first arrow may come back to see it.

success.text: You rub the arrow out with your sleeve and chalk a new one pointing back up toward daylight, and another at every turning between here and the cave mouth, low on the wall where a child's eyes would find it. It takes you the whole day. Your sleeve is white to the elbow.

choices.label: Go down a little way with a lamp
choices.intent: You have spent years not knowing. Find out.
choices.risk: The bottom of that stair is the thing you ran from.

success.text: Forty steps down there is a room with a long table laid for supper and nobody at it, and on every plate a candle, burning. You count the plates. You count them twice. Then you climb back into the cold with the number in your mouth and write it on the wall at the top of the stair, so the next one who comes will know.

failure.text: Twenty steps down the lamp gutters, and the dark fills with the smell of warm bread and a voice that knows exactly how tired you are. You sit down on the step. You do not remember standing up again. When you come back to the crossroads a day has gone, and you are very hungry.

cards.title: A Habit Still Worth Something
cards.flavor: You still wear the habit because it is the only coat you have, and at the fortified camp it opens every door. Soldiers touch their caps. A sergeant asks you to come to the long tent and say the words over three of his who will not see morning; they believe a sister's blessing goes with them past the Verge. You believed it too, once. You do not know what you believe now.

choices.label: Say the words you were taught
choices.intent: Give them the blessing they are asking for, whatever it is worth.
choices.risk: The words still sound like her voice.

success.text: You kneel by each cot and say the words in your own voice, slowly, as if you were teaching them to yourself. The third soldier holds your paw until the end. Afterward the sergeant gives you his ration and calls you Sister, and for the first time in your life it does not sound like a leash.

failure.text: Halfway through, your throat closes and you cannot find the rest. You hold the soldier's paw instead and hum the tune that went under the words. It is enough for him. It is not enough for you.

choices.label: Tell them you are no sister
choices.intent: Say it before you say anything else.
choices.risk: The sergeant needs a sister, not the truth.

success.text: "I walked out," you say. "I'm nobody's sister." The sergeant looks at you a long time, then asks if you will sit with them anyway. You do, all night, without one word of the old prayers, and it is the first true thing you have ever done in a habit.

choices.label: Cut the habit into bandages
choices.intent: The camp is short of linen. You are short of reasons to wear it.
choices.risk: The nights here are bitter, and it is the only coat you have.

success.text: You go behind the long tent with a borrowed knife and cut the grey wool into strips, and boil them, and roll them, and carry them to the camp physician in your arms, shivering in your shirtsleeves. She keeps all but three rolls and gives you a soldier's old coat for them. It fits worse, and it is yours.

choices.label: Sell blessings for bread
choices.intent: Every soldier in this camp is frightened, and frightened folk pay.
choices.risk: You know whose trick this is.

success.text: You go tent to tent with a sweet face and the words you were taught, and every soldier pays a crust or a coin for them. By morning your pack is full. You eat well that week. You notice you have started folding your paws the way the Abbess folded hers.

failure.text: The third soldier you bless laughs in your face. "My mother paid for those," he says. "Paid her whole life." He throws the crust at your feet anyway, and you pick it up.

cards.title: The Seep Nobody Has Claimed
cards.flavor: Your seep is a green crack in the delta mud, a mile off the road behind a stand of dead reeds, and it gives a jar an hour if you are patient. Nobody else knows it. This morning, filling jars, you hear a cough from the road: a gopher family sitting by a dead ox, their kit licking dew off a wagon wheel. They have not seen you, or the seep. They will see your black coat in a minute.

choices.label: Show them the seep
choices.intent: Walk them through the reeds and let them drink for nothing, forever.
choices.risk: That green crack is your whole living.

success.text: You lead them through the dead reeds and show them the crack and how to wait on it. The father drinks lying on his belly with his eyes shut. By noon there are three more families at your seep, and by dusk a cairn by the road pointing to it. You still have this morning's jars. You will have to find another living.

choices.label: Sell them a blessed jar
choices.intent: Ring the bell, do the patter, take what they can spare.
choices.risk: They will spare more than they can.

success.text: You ring your little bell and hold the jar up to the sun so it shines, and tell them the sisters to the south blessed it. The father pays with a hand plane and a sack of meal. The kit drinks first. Then they walk on south, toward the sisters you named, because you named them.

choices.label: Carry jars to them all day
choices.intent: Don't show them the seep. Don't charge them either. Just walk.
choices.risk: A mile each way in the delta sun, all day long.

success.text: You carry jar after jar the mile from the seep to the road, and call them blessed, and charge nothing. By evening the ox is the only one not drinking. The father asks what order you belong to. The order of fools, you tell him, and ring your bell, and he laughs, and that is payment of a kind.

failure.text: By the fourth trip the sun has your head ringing louder than your bell. You fall beside the dead ox, and the gophers pour your own blessed water over your face and ears until you can stand. They help you carry the jars back. Somehow, on the way, they find the seep.

cards.title: A Sister's Purse at the Fence
cards.flavor: At a border farm a sister on a grey mule waits for you by the fence, as if she knew your road. Inside the farmhouse a kit is coughing. The sister has heard of the hare brother who sells water blessed by her house, and she does not mind the lie, she says. She holds out a purse that clinks: one coin for every family you send south to the sisters with a sick child. The farm wife is listening at the door.

choices.label: Take the purse
choices.intent: Send them south. The sisters will feed them, she says, and pay you for the kindness.
choices.risk: You have watched the mission road. Nothing comes back down it but water casks.

success.text: You take the purse and tell the farm wife, warmly, that the sisters to the south will have her kit right by spring. She thanks you, and gives you a jar of honey for the advice. In the morning the cart goes south with the sister on her mule riding behind it, and you ring your bell over the empty yard out of habit.

choices.label: Refuse her in front of the family
choices.intent: Tell the farm wife what the sister is buying, plainly, with your own lie in it.
choices.risk: A con man against a habit. Guess who they believe.

success.text: You tell the farm wife that you sell creek water with a bell rung over it, and that the sister is paying you to send sick kits to a house nobody comes back from. Both in one breath. The farm wife looks from your coat to the habit and shuts the door on you both. Later, through the window, you see her steeping willow bark.

failure.text: The farm wife hears a peddler call a sister a liar, and that settles it. She orders you off her land, and the sister smiles at you over the fence as you go. You don't know which way the cart will go in the morning, and you don't go back to find out.

choices.label: Take the purse, then warn them off
choices.intent: Rob the sisters, and tell the farm the truth once she has gone.
choices.risk: If she catches you, every sister on every road will know your bell.

success.text: You take the purse with a bow and wait until the mule is out of sight. Then you knock and tell the farm wife: whatever she does, don't go south. You leave her three of the sister's coins for bark. It is the best con you have ever pulled, and the first one you are proud of.
