failure.text: The sister doubles back for her gloves and finds you on the farm step with her purse in your paw and the truth in your mouth. She takes the purse back without a word. She does not need one. The farm wife heard, though, and the cart stays in the yard.

choices.label: Ring your bell over the kit and go
choices.intent: Bless the child for free and stay out of the rest.
choices.risk: Walking away is also a choice.

success.text: You ring your little bell over the coughing kit and say the blessing, and charge nothing, and walk off down the road before the sister can say anything else. You never learn which way the cart went. You notice you are walking very fast.

cards.title: Blessed by the Brother Himself
cards.flavor: In the stone hollow a young vole in a black coat too big for him is selling jars of drip-pool water to the cave folk. Blessed, he cries, by the hare brother of the south road, and he rings a little tin bell exactly like yours. He has your patter down to the pauses. He does not know your face. Two children who drank from his jars yesterday are coughing against the wall, and the pool he fills from is green.

choices.label: Expose him, and yourself with him
choices.intent: Tell the hollow there is no blessing, from him or from you.
choices.risk: The hollow will want somebody to pay.

success.text: You stand on a salt barrel and tell the hollow that you are the hare brother, that the blessing was always a bell and a story and creek water, and that his water isn't even clean. The cave folk pour his jars into the dust. Then they look at you a long time, decide that a liar who confesses is a novelty, and let you sleep by the fire.

failure.text: The hollow hears two liars in black coats and finds it wants neither. They take his jars and yours and chase you both up the passage with stones. Outside, in the wind, the vole asks if you could teach him the bit where you hold it up to the sun.

choices.label: Teach him to boil it
choices.intent: If he is going to sell your lie, at least make him sell clean water.
choices.risk: You are teaching a boy your trade.

success.text: You take him aside and show him how to boil the water and let it settle and pour off the top, and which pools never to touch. He listens like a novice. The next day his jars are clear, the coughing children are no worse, and the patter is exactly the same. You are not sure what you have made. It is better than what was there.

failure.text: He thinks you want a cut and runs off with his jars before you can explain. You spend the day boiling the green pool yourself and handing it out in his place, ringing your bell, and the hollow cannot tell you apart.

choices.label: Buy him out and run it yourself
choices.intent: Take his jars, his patch and his customers. You do it better.
choices.risk: Two children are already coughing on his water.

success.text: You trade him a day's food for his jars, his bell and his patch, and he goes off glad. You fill from a clean seep higher up and do a better patter than he ever could, and the hollow pays you twice what it paid him. Nobody mentions the two coughing children against the wall, including you.

choices.label: Let his lie stand
choices.intent: It is the same lie as yours. Who are you to call it?
choices.risk: His water is not the same as yours.

success.text: You buy one of his jars for the look of it, pour it out behind a rock, and go on your way. On the way out you pass the two coughing children and do not stop. Your bell rings with every step, and for once you wish it wouldn't.

cards.title: The Widow on the Black Glass
cards.flavor: On the black glass road a prairie dog mother is hauling a handcart with three young ones riding on the sacks. You know her before she knows you. At a burned waystation a long way back she gave you her wedding ring for a jar of water for her sick father. It is still in your coat. You never could sell it. Then she hears your bell, and stops, and turns round.

choices.label: Give back the ring
choices.intent: Put it in her paw before she can say anything.
choices.risk: There is nothing to say that makes it square.

success.text: You hold it out on your open palm. She looks at it a long time before she takes it, and slides it back on, and it is loose now. "He lived till the rains," she says. "He said your water tasted like rain." She doesn't thank you. She lets you push the handcart up the next rise, which is better.

choices.label: Tell her it was only water
choices.intent: She deserves to know what she paid for.
choices.risk: She may need it to have been something.

success.text: "It was seep water," you say. "Green and a little salty. I rang a bell over it." She nods slowly. "I knew," she says. "He knew too. He drank it anyway, and laughed, first time in a month." She walks on. You stand on the black glass a while, holding a ring you forgot to give back.

failure.text: The words come out wrong, and what she hears is that her father died on swamp water and a stranger's joke. She hits you once, hard, and walks on with her children staring back at you over the sacks. You deserved it. It does not help either of you.

choices.label: Sell her one more jar for the road
choices.intent: She will need water on the glass. You have water.
choices.risk: She has nothing left to pay with but what is on the cart.

success.text: You do the patter, softer than usual, and she pays with a sack of seed she was saving for wherever they stop. The young ones drink. She does not ask about her father, and you do not offer. The ring stays in your coat, heavier than before.

choices.label: Walk with them to the next camp
choices.intent: Push the cart. Carry the smallest. Ring the bell when they flag.
choices.risk: The black glass cuts feet and slows everyone.

success.text: You walk with them two days to the fortified camp, pushing the handcart and telling the young ones stories about blessed water in which you are always the fool. At the camp gate the mother finds the ring in her coat pocket, where you slipped it while she slept. She looks back, and you are already ringing your bell at somebody else.

failure.text: The glass opens your boots on the first day and your feet on the second. You get them to the camp a day late, limping, and the mother wraps your feet herself without a word, which is how you know she has recognized the bell.

cards.title: A Feather Under Glass
cards.flavor: The trader keeps a black feather under a glass dome on his counter and swears a Storm Crow grew it: hold it to your eye and see your lost. An otter father traded his mule for it and stands pressing it to his face, seeing nothing. You know that feather. It came out of your own wing the night you flew from the cave. He sees the ash on you, and asks you to look for his daughter, gone three weeks down the mission road.

choices.label: Name the price before you look
choices.intent: Tell him plainly what sight costs, and let him choose which memory to pay with.
choices.risk: Knowing the price, he may not pay it, and then you both go hungry.

success.text: You tell him before you look: a memory, his choice which. He thinks a long time and gives you a bad winter he would rather lose. Then you look. She is alive, behind a convent wall, in a bed with clean sheets. He does not like the clean sheets any more than you do.

failure.text: You name the price and he pays it, and the sight shows you only a wall and a bell that hangs without a clapper. You give him back what he paid. It is the first time in forty years you have made change.

choices.label: Look for nothing in return
choices.intent: Pay for the sight yourself, out of what little you still remember.
choices.risk: Sight nobody pays for is paid by the one who sees.

success.text: You look without asking anything, and the price comes out of you instead: a morning in the cave when you were small, gone like a lamp blown out. In its place you see his daughter, alive, behind a convent wall. He weeps and thanks you. You cannot remember what you lost, only that it was warm.

choices.label: Take the coven's price, the old way
choices.intent: Take the memory he would least want to give. That is the one that buys true sight.
choices.risk: This is the price you burned the book to stop taking.

success.text: You take the day she was born. It slides onto your string as a warm bead, and the sight it buys is sharp as glass: the convent, the dormitory, her bed. You tell him all of it. He thanks you, then frowns at the road as if he cannot quite picture who he is walking toward. He presses bread on you anyway. You take that too.

choices.label: Show the trader the gap in your wing
choices.intent: Spread your wing on his counter so he can see where his feather came from.
choices.risk: A trader caught selling a Storm Crow's feather has a coven to answer to, and may decide you are easier.

success.text: You spread your wing across his counter and lay the feather in the gap. It fits like a key. The trader goes grey under his whiskers, gives the otter back his mule, and asks you, very politely, not to tell anyone in the cave where you found it.

failure.text: The trader laughs at the old bird with the bald wing and says every crow on the road claims his feathers. The otter believes him, because he has to. You leave with nothing but the cold in the gap where the feather used to be.

cards.title: A Reading for the Abbess
cards.flavor: The Abbess herself meets you at the refuge gate with a warm loaf and a cup of milk. A Storm Crow at her table is a blessing, she says; would you read the year ahead for the house and its children? She will pay in bread and a bed. Behind her the chapel bell hangs with no clapper, and when you try to look at her straight, your sight slides off her face like rain off oilcloth.

choices.label: Read her true, at her own table
choices.intent: Look past the milk and the manners, and say what you see out loud.
choices.risk: She is the most patient creature you have ever met, and she has a long memory.

success.text: You look until your eyes water, and it gives: something coiled and waiting behind the chapel wall, and her hand feeding it. You say so at supper, in front of the novices. The Abbess smiles and has you shown to the road with a loaf for the journey. One young otter in a novice's veil follows you to the gate, white as the milk.

failure.text: Your sight slides off her again and you see only a kind old otter with a crumb on her habit. She thanks you warmly. You sleep in the guest bed and wake with a ring of black candle wax on the sill that was not there when you lay down.

choices.label: Read her a good year and eat
choices.intent: Tell her what she wants to hear. Rain in spring, full cribs, a quiet winter.
choices.risk: A false reading under that roof may be the worst price you have ever taken.

success.text: You tell her rain in spring and full cribs, and she is delighted, and you eat better than you have in a month. In the night the dormitory is very quiet. You lie awake listening to it and tell yourself a reading is only words.

choices.label: Leave a feather under every pillow
choices.intent: A Storm Crow feather shows a true face to whoever holds it. Pluck enough for the dormitory.
choices.risk: Every feather you pull is a feather you do not fly on.

success.text: While the house sings vespers you go down the dormitory and slide a black feather under each small pillow, wincing at every pull. In the morning, from the road, you look back. A row of small faces watches the Abbess cross the yard from the dormitory window, and not one of them is smiling.

cards.title: Someone on Your Old Perch
cards.flavor: The dead tree at the fork of the canyon trail was your perch for nine years. A young crow sits on it now, her flight feathers still cave-grey, selling sight to a line of drovers. She is quick and she is good, and she is taking the coven's price without telling anyone what it is: a drover walks away from her wiping his eyes and not knowing why. She sees the ash on you and goes still. "They said you were dead," she says.

choices.label: Teach her to say the price first
choices.intent: Sit on the branch beside her and show her how it is done honestly.
choices.risk: She is young, and the coven's way fills a belly faster.

success.text: You sit beside her all afternoon. When the next drover comes she tells him the price before she looks, and he thinks about it, and decides not to pay, and she lets him walk on. She looks at you as if you had shown her a door she did not know was there.

failure.text: She listens politely, the way you once listened to the coven, and nods in all the right places. Before you are out of sight you hear her take the next drover's price the old way, quick and quiet.

choices.label: Send her home to the cave
choices.intent: Tell her to go back before the road teaches her what it taught you.
choices.risk: She will tell the coven where you perch.

success.text: "Go home," you tell her, "before the road makes you old." Something in your voice does it. She flies north toward the deep cave in the evening, and you know she will tell them you are alive. You find you do not mind.

failure.text: She laughs at you, not unkindly, and says the coven will be glad to hear their old book-burner is begging at crossroads. Then she takes the next drover's price right in front of you.

choices.label: Take your perch back
choices.intent: The young give way to the old. Climb up, and charge in bread, which is honest.
choices.risk: You are teaching her by example, whatever you choose.

success.text: You hop up and she gives way, as the young always do. The drovers' line moves to you. You charge a heel of bread a reading, which is honest, and you eat for the first time in two days. She sits on the lowest branch and watches exactly how you do it.

choices.label: Give the drover back what she took
choices.intent: Buy the bead from her and blow the memory back into the drover's ear.
choices.risk: No Storm Crow gives back a price. The coven will hear that, too.

success.text: You pay her a day's bread for the new bead, crack it in your beak, and blow it into the drover's ear. He sits down hard in the dust with his wife's face back in his head. The fledgling stares. "You can do that?" she says. You can. Nobody ever wanted to.

cards.title: The Coven Keeps a Stool
cards.flavor: Three crow-witches sit in the cave mouth out of the hail, black shawls pulled to their beaks, and they have kept a fourth stool empty. They knew you were coming; they always do. The eldest holds out a new tally book, its pages blank, its binding the same as the one you burned in the deep lamp. "Write one debt in it," she says. "Any debt you like. Then you can come home."

choices.label: Tell them why you burned the book
choices.intent: Say it to their faces at last: a ledger that never closes is a cage.
choices.risk: They have had forty years to decide you were wrong.

success.text: You tell them about the debtors who could never pay, the children born owing, the book that only ever grew. The hail stops while you talk. When you finish, the youngest of them sets her own string of beads on the empty stool, and the eldest closes the blank book without a word.

failure.text: They hear you out in silence, as they heard you out the night you burned it. The stool stays empty. You walk back out into the hail with your say said, which is not nothing, and your feathers soaked to the quill.

choices.label: Write your own name, owing
choices.intent: Give them their one debt: yours, to them, for the book you burned.
choices.risk: A debt in that book is never quite paid.

success.text: You take the pen and write your own name, owing, in a small clear hand. The eldest reads it and nods, and the youngest moves over so you can sit. The cave is warm and dry and smells of home, and you sleep on your old stool the whole night through, a debtor among sisters.

choices.label: Break your string of beads into the draft
choices.intent: Every bead round your neck is a memory you were paid. Let them all go home.
choices.risk: Without the string, you are just an old crow with ash on her wings.

success.text: You crack the beads one by one in your beak and let the cave's draft carry each memory out over the land, to whoever it was taken from. It takes until dark. Your neck feels light and cold. Not one of the three witches speaks; no Storm Crow has ever given back the price before.

cards.title: The Writ Read at the Landing
cards.flavor: The ferry pilot remembers a one-eyed coyote crossing four days back, and says he might remember more for a price. You unfold the writ on his barrel head and read it aloud, every word, the way you always do: one year of water from the Dustwater water house, for the coyote, brought in alive. The pilot's wife stops coiling rope. "Alive," she says. "That's new. The last two hunters' papers said otherwise."

choices.label: Pay the pilot for the trail
choices.intent: Pay what he asks and get the trail while it is still warm.
choices.risk: A trail you pay for can be sold twice.

success.text: He pockets your food and tells you: upriver, toward the dry delta, poling his own passage because he had no fare. He also says the coyote asked which road the water house's night wagons take these days. You write it in your book under the coyote's name, and wonder why a wanted man would want to know.

choices.label: Ask the wife about the other hunters
choices.intent: Find out who else carried paper on him, and what it said.
choices.risk: You may not like who you are working beside.

success.text: Two hunters before you, she says, with water house papers marked dead and paid double for it. Neither came back this way. The coyote, when he crossed, asked her which road the night wagons take, and she did not know what he meant until she saw his face. You write it all down, and leave the writ folded for the rest of the day.

failure.text: She goes back to her rope and will not say more to a hunter. All you get is the look she gives your writ: the look mothers gave you years ago, when you served whatever paper you were handed and never read the dates.

choices.label: Lean on him as an accessory
choices.intent: Remind him that ferrying a wanted coyote can be written up too.
choices.risk: Threats are a kind of lie, and you do not tell those.

success.text: You tell him, quietly, what a writ for harboring looks like. He does not need to see one. He gives you the trail for nothing, upriver toward the dry delta, and spits in the water when you go. You write his name in your book on a line by itself, and you do not like seeing it there.

failure.text: He laughs at you. "Write it, then," he says, and pushes off with a boatload of passengers who all heard. By evening every landing on the river knows the badger with the writ makes threats now. You find the trail yourself, a day late and a meal short.

choices.label: Nail a copy to the landing post
choices.intent: Let the whole river know who you hunt and why. That is how you work.
choices.risk: He will know you are coming.

success.text: You copy the writ in your square hand and nail it to the landing post with your own name signed under it. Nobody comes forward. By evening someone has written beneath it in charcoal, in a child's careful letters: ask him what he took. You read that twice, and copy it into your book.

cards.title: Supper Before the Writ
cards.flavor: The farm wife sets a plate for you before she knows what you do for a living. Halfway through supper you recognize the farmer from the second writ in your satchel: Amos Pell, two sacks of seed owed to the land office, to be brought in alive. He sees you see it. His three kits keep eating. Nobody at the table says anything for a long time, and then his wife passes you the bread.

choices.label: Serve it after supper
choices.intent: Finish the meal you were given, then read him the writ outside, as you always do.
choices.risk: The kits will watch you walk their father down the lane.

success.text: You thank her for the meal, and you mean it. Then you take him out to the yard and read him every word. He walks beside you down the lane in the morning without being held. The kits stand at the fence. The land office pays you in flour, and it is good flour.

choices.label: Pay the two sacks out of your own fee
choices.intent: Write the debt satisfied, and sign your name to it.
choices.risk: You will be two sacks short on a long road.

success.text: You count out what you have and write satisfied across the writ in your square hand, and sign it, and date it. Amos reads it three times. His wife cries into the dishwater where the kits cannot see. You ride on in the morning lighter and hungrier, and it is the best line in your book.

choices.label: Read the writ closely by the lamp
choices.intent: Check every date and figure, the way you have since the boy on the quarry writ.
choices.risk: You might find nothing, and then you will have to choose.

success.text: The land office charged the drought tithe twice, once in spring and once at harvest, and wrote the second one up as seed. Amos owes nothing. You write the land office a letter with the dates in it, sign it, and tear the writ in half at the table so the kits can watch it happen.

failure.text: The figures are clean. The debt is real. You sit with the lamp until it gutters, and when you look up Amos is sitting across from you, waiting to hear what kind of hunter you are.

choices.label: Feed it to the stove
choices.intent: Burn it, and write lost in your book.
choices.risk: It would be the first lie your book has ever held.

success.text: The writ goes up fast, like all paper. In your book, under Amos Pell, you write lost, and the word sits there on the page looking back at you. Eleven years of writs and that is the first lie in them. The kits sleep. Their father sits up with you till dawn and does not know what to say.

cards.title: The Company's Runaway
cards.flavor: The quarry clerk meets you at the rim with a writ already filled in and a fee that would feed you for a year: one runaway apprentice, twelve years old, bound for nine more. The boy is not hard to find. He is on a ledge below the company store, splitting stone for a family who feed him, and he is very good at it. The clerk is watching to see what kind of hunter you are.

choices.label: Serve the writ; the paper is good
choices.intent: It is dated, sealed and signed. That has always been enough.
choices.risk: You served a boy's writ once before. You remember how that ended.

success.text: It is a good writ: dated, sealed, signed with his mother's mark. You read it to him the way you read every writ, and he climbs the ledge beside you without being held. The clerk counts your fee into your paw. You write the boy's name in your book with the date and the price, and it looks exactly like every other line.

choices.label: Hand the writ back unserved
choices.intent: You do not serve paper on children. Not anymore.
choices.risk: The clerk has other hunters, and they are not particular.

success.text: You hand it back folded. The clerk shrugs and says there are other hunters. You tell him their names, because you know them, and what each one charges, and that every one of them will hear from you first. Then you go down to the ledge and tell the family too. Honest is honest.

choices.label: Go down to the ledge first
choices.intent: Warn the family, then climb back up and tell the clerk the truth.
choices.risk: The company has its own way of answering hunters who change sides.

success.text: The family moves the boy out by the ore road before noon. You climb back to the rim and tell the clerk exactly what you did and why, and that you will swear to it before any magistrate he likes. He tears up nothing. He only writes your name in a book of his own.

failure.text: The clerk was watching from the rim and sends two company men down the ledge after you. You stand in the path with your coat open until the family is out of sight, and the men leave you on the stones to think about it.

choices.label: Buy out his nine years
choices.intent: Offer the clerk what you carry for the paper itself.
choices.risk: It is more than you can spare, and he knows it.

success.text: The clerk weighs your sack against nine years and decides the company would rather eat now. He sells you the writ. You walk down to the ledge and give it to the boy, show him the place on the paper where the word served goes, and let him write it himself.

cards.title: The Coyote at Last
cards.flavor: You find him at last in the fortified camp, sitting on an upturned bucket outside the closed infirmary with his hat in his paws: the one-eyed coyote, thinner than his notice, too tired to run. He sees the writ in your coat before he sees your face, and stands up slowly with his paws open. "Read it to me," he says. "I heard you always do."

choices.label: Read it and take him in
choices.intent: You have walked four lands on this paper. Finish it.
choices.risk: A year of water in Dustwater, and a coyote in the water house lockup.

success.text: You read it to him, every word, and he listens with his head bowed as if it were a sermon. He does not run. In the morning you start back for Dustwater together, and neither of you says much. The writ is good. You did what the writ said. You find you have stopped liking the sound of that.

choices.label: Ask him what he really took
choices.intent: Hear his side before you serve the writ, and check it against your book.
choices.risk: A wanted coyote has had a long time to work on his story.

success.text: He tells you about the night wagons, the gate past the canyons, the canvas he finally looked under, and the lock he shot on his way out of town. You check every date he gives against your book, and against the two hunters whose papers said dead, and every one of them fits. Under his name you write: writ served on the wrong party.

failure.text: He tells it badly, the way true things often come out, and you cannot be sure. You sit across from him all night by the infirmary wall with the writ still folded in your coat, and in the morning you are both still there, and neither of you has decided anything.

choices.label: Swear out a writ on the water house
choices.intent: Take what you know to the camp magistrate and turn the paper round.
choices.risk: Water houses own magistrates. This one might be the exception.

success.text: The magistrate reads your book for an hour by lamplight. Then she draws up a writ of her own, sealed and dated, naming the Dustwater water house and its night wagons, and hands it to you to serve. It is the heaviest paper you have ever carried. You fold the coyote's writ inside it.

failure.text: The magistrate hears you out, sighs, and tells you the water house supplies her camp. She will not seal anything. You walk out with your book under your arm, and the coyote is still waiting on his bucket.

choices.label: Tear the writ and give him half
choices.intent: Let him carry proof that one hunter stopped.
choices.risk: The water house will only write another, and send someone worse.

success.text: You tear it down the middle, through the seal, and give him the half with his name on it. He looks at it a long time. In your book you write torn, and the date, and sign your own name under it, and that is no lie at all. He walks out of camp at dusk. You do not watch which way.

cards.title: The Deed in Your Coat
cards.flavor: The deed to the Dustwater water rights is folded in your coat, and the ferry is halfway across when the shouting starts on the landing behind you. Your foreman, Pruitt, a lean weasel with the water house keys still on his belt, has the pilot pole back. "You can walk off, Mr. Vane," he says, loud enough for the whole landing. "You can't walk off with the water."

choices.label: Sign it over to the town, here
choices.intent: Every cup of Dustwater's water to Dustwater, signed on a barrel head where the whole landing can watch.
choices.risk: Pruitt has eleven guards who are paid in that water.

success.text: You sign it on a barrel head with the landing watching: the water of Dustwater to the town of Dustwater, every cup, no tickets. Pruitt laughs, then reads it, then stops laughing. A rabbit woman takes the deed out of your paw before he can, folds it into her apron, and does not thank you.

choices.label: Sell him the deed
choices.intent: He wants it. You want to be gone. Name a price.
choices.risk: He will run it the way you taught him.

success.text: He pays in water tickets and dried meat, more than the deed is worth to anyone who means to do right with it. You shake his paw on the landing. He will run the water house exactly the way you taught him, and you knew that before you named your price.

choices.label: Tell the landing what the water cost
choices.intent: Say out loud, to all of them, what you traded the mission for its spring.
choices.risk: Some of them drank that water. Some of them sent you children.

success.text: You tell it all: the drought, the mission's spring, Mother's terms, eleven children by name. The landing goes quiet as a church. Nobody spits. That is worse. When you finish, Pruitt has slipped away, and the ferry pilot poles you across without taking your fare and will not look at you.

failure.text: You get as far as the word mission and Pruitt talks over you, about drought and hard bargains and a baron who kept the town alive. The landing nods along. The ferry pulls out with the rest of it still in your mouth, where it has been for four years.

choices.label: Keep the deed folded and cross
choices.intent: A deed is only paper until someone needs it. You may need it.
choices.risk: Pruitt will run the water house without it, and worse.

success.text: You tell the pilot to keep poling, and he does, because you are still the baron for one more mile. Pruitt shouts himself hoarse on the landing. The deed stays warm against your chest all the way over. You tell yourself you are keeping it safe.

cards.title: The Benefactor's Plate
cards.flavor: There is a brass plate on the refuge gatepost thanking you, by name, for your generosity to the orphans of Dustwater. You paid for the brass. The sister at the gate knows you before you reach it, and her face lights up. Mother has kept your chair, she says. The children are at supper. You may see them, if you like, once you have spoken with Mother.

choices.label: Ask to see the ledger
choices.intent: Get the names of the eleven you sent, and where each one went.
choices.risk: Mother keeps her books close, and her sisters closer.

success.text: She brings a ledger with your mark on every page and leaves you alone with it, because you are the benefactor. You copy the names onto the back of your deed: eleven of them, and beside nine, no line for where they went. You thank her. Your paw does not shake until you are out of sight.

failure.text: Mother keeps the ledger, the sister says, and Mother will be so glad to show you after supper. You leave before supper with nothing written down, and the sister waves you off from the gate as if you will be back.

choices.label: Pry your name off the gatepost
choices.intent: Take your name off their gate, where every traveler reads it.
choices.risk: The sisters will see. So will anyone they tell.

success.text: The screws come out stiff, and then the plate comes away in your paw. You throw it in the ditch beside the road, face up, so anyone walking past can see what used to hang there. The sister watches you from the gate with her lamp and does not try to stop you.

failure.text: The plate will not come. You tear your knuckles on the screws until two sisters come out with a lamp and take you, very kindly, by the arms, and walk you down the road. They are so sorry you are unwell. Your name stays on the gate.

choices.label: Speak with Mother
choices.intent: Sit in the chair she kept for you, and hear what she has to say.
choices.risk: You know what she has to say. You have always known.

success.text: She pours tea and speaks gently of the drought ahead, and of the deep spring, which could flow to whoever holds the deed. She asks only for the names of families on the road who cannot feed their children. You write three. It is so easy. It was always easy. She thanks you for your generosity, and a sister fills your skins to the brim.

cards.title: Eleven Candles and One
cards.flavor: Deep in the candle court a crow clerk leads you to a niche you did not know you owned. Eleven short candles burn in a row, each scratched with a child's name, and behind them burns a tall one scratched with yours. An unpaid oath, she says: your bargain with the mission. While the tall flame stands, the small ones are bound to it. She holds out a brass snuffer, and names her price for using it.

choices.label: Pay what she asks and snuff it
choices.intent: She wants a year off the end of your life. It seems cheap.
choices.risk: Witch prices are never only what they say.

success.text: She takes the year the way a crow takes a seed, quick and without looking at you, and you feel it go. Then she hands you the snuffer. The tall flame dies with a smell like a wet ledger. Down the row the eleven small ones lean once and stand straight, burning on their own now, steady as stars.

choices.label: Sit and read every name aloud
choices.intent: Kneel at the niche and say each name until the night is over.
choices.risk: Some of these you only ever knew as figures in a ledger.

success.text: You say them all night, eleven names over and over, until you remember which one stammered and which one was afraid of the dark, because you knew, you always knew. By dawn you can say them without looking. You copy them onto the back of your deed in your own hand.

failure.text: At the seventh name you cannot remember whether it was a boy or a girl. You try for an hour. The clerk brings you a cup of water and says nothing, which is the worst kindness anyone has ever done you. You copy the names down anyway, all eleven, the seventh with a mark beside it.

choices.label: Offer her the deed instead
choices.intent: Water is worth more than a year of anybody's life. See if she agrees.
choices.risk: A witch who owns a town's water is not a kinder master than a baron.

success.text: She reads the deed with real interest. Water, she says, is a fine thing to own. She tucks it under her wing and snuffs the tall candle herself, and the eleven small flames stand straight on their own. The water of Dustwater belongs to a crow-witch now. You cannot say whether that is better.

failure.text: She laughs, a dry clatter. Paper is not a price, she says. A price is something you will miss. She hands the deed back, and the tall candle burns on behind the eleven small ones, and you climb out of the court with your coat no lighter.

cards.title: A Cup From Her Line
cards.flavor: At the last gate a young sister in a grey apron is ladling water to the line from a mission barrel, and she knows you. You wrote her name in a ledger four years ago, when she was nine. She looks at your coat, your face, the corner of the deed showing at your pocket, and keeps ladling. "You're in my line, Mr. Vane," she says. "Everybody gets a cup."

choices.label: Tell her what you did
choices.intent: Not to be forgiven. Only so that someone she can see has said it.
choices.risk: She may already know. She may not.

success.text: You tell her about the drought, the spring and the ledger, plainly, standing in the line with everybody listening. She keeps ladling all the way through. When you finish she hands you your cup, full to the brim, and says she knows, and that she is not the one you owe. Then she tells you who is.

failure.text: You start, and she stops you with the ladle raised. "Not here," she says. "Not to me." The line shuffles forward around you. You drink your cup and stand at the edge of the yard with the rest of it unsaid, cooling in your chest.

choices.label: Give her the deed
choices.intent: Put the water rights of Dustwater in the paws of someone you sold for them.
choices.risk: It may be the cruellest thing you have done yet, or the only right one.

success.text: You hold it out. She reads it slowly, the whole thing, with the ladle still in her other paw. Then she folds it into her apron pocket and goes on serving the line. She does not thank you, and you did not want her to. A town's water has a new owner, and she knows exactly what it cost.

choices.label: Go to the back of the line
choices.intent: Wait your turn like everybody else, however long it takes.
choices.risk: It is a long line, and the sun is high.

success.text: You walk to the very end of the line and stand there all afternoon in the glare, behind a ferret family and an old ewe with a cough. Nobody makes way for you. When your turn comes she ladles you a cup like anybody's, and you drink it like anybody, and it is the best water you have ever tasted.

choices.label: Ask her where the others are
choices.intent: She may know where the rest of the eleven went.
choices.risk: She may not want to tell the one who sent them.

success.text: She gives you four names you know, and where they are now: two at the threshold camp, one working the river, one who never left the mission. She does not give you the rest, and you do not ask. You write the four beside the names on your deed, and that night you start walking toward the nearest.

failure.text: She looks at you a long moment and says they are where you sent them. Then she ladles the next cup. It is not an answer. It is the only one you are owed.

cards.title: The Foreman's Offer
cards.flavor: Your husband's name is still chalked on the debt board at the quarry rim, and under it, in newer chalk, is yours. The foreman knows you: the guide off the canyon ledge. Six debtors walked off the rock last week into the canyon forks, where his catchers lose every trail by noon. They left little cairns for each other, he says. Read them for him, and he will wipe the board clean with his own sleeve.

choices.label: Read their cairns for him
choices.intent: Clear the debt, so Wenna and Pip never see their names on that board.
choices.risk: Six debtors have children too.

success.text: It takes you half a day. Three stones and a flat one, pointing to a seep. Two and a split stone, meaning wait here. You show the catchers where, and by dark the six come back up the switchbacks roped together, not looking at you. The foreman wipes the board with his sleeve, as promised. The chalk dust stays on his cuff a long time.

choices.label: Read them wrong on purpose
choices.intent: Take the catchers up the forks and lose them where the runaways never went.
choices.risk: The foreman is no fool, and he knows you know these forks better than anyone.

success.text: You read every cairn backwards, slowly and with great care, and walk the catchers into a box canyon two days from anywhere. They come out footsore and blaming each other. The foreman pays you a day's food for your trouble and never once suspects. Somewhere out in the forks, six debtors are still walking.

failure.text: The head catcher reads a little himself, enough to see the stones say something other than what you say. He walks you back to the rim, and the foreman adds a line under your name in fresh chalk. Wenna watches him do it.

choices.label: Ask to see the ledger first
choices.intent: Before you bargain over a debt, find out what the debt is.
choices.risk: The ledger belongs to the company, and so does the rock you are standing on.

success.text: He lets you look, because he thinks you cannot read. You can. Corran's debt is there in a clerk's hand, and beside it the interest, and beside that a charge for his own burial. It has been paid twice already. You say so in front of the whole shift, and the foreman does not reach for the chalk again while you are there.

failure.text: The ledger is a thicket of figures you cannot make sense of fast enough, and the foreman shuts it on your finger. "Read your stones, guide," he says. "Leave the paper to them as can."

choices.label: Walk away from the board
choices.intent: Take the children and go. The debt can follow you if it has legs.
choices.risk: It has legs. They are the company's.

success.text: You take Pip on your hip and Wenna by the paw and walk off the rim without answering him. Nobody stops you. The names stay on the board behind you, his and yours, and you feel them on the back of your neck the whole way down the switchbacks.

cards.title: The Agent's List
cards.flavor: The quarry company has sent a clerk to the ferry landing with a folding table and a list: debtors who may not cross the river until their accounts are settled. Your husband's name is on it, struck through, and yours is written underneath. Below yours, in the same careful hand, are two more lines. Wenna. Pip. Your daughter reads them before you can get your hoof over the page.

choices.label: Give your mother's name
choices.intent: Cross as somebody else, with two children who could be anybody's.
choices.risk: If he asks Wenna her name, she will tell him the truth. You raised her to.

success.text: You give your mother's name and your mother's village, and the clerk looks for it and does not find it. Wenna holds her tongue all the way across the river, and on the far bank she starts crying, from the effort of holding it. You hold her until she stops.

failure.text: The clerk asks Wenna her name, kindly, and she tells him. He does not raise his voice. He only turns the list round so you can see your own names again, and asks you to stand aside for the next in line.

choices.label: Ask him what the law says about children
choices.intent: Make him say out loud whether a dead father's debt can pass to a child.
choices.risk: If the law says yes, you have just made him look it up.

success.text: He goes red, then checks his own book. It does not, not in this territory, not to anyone under sixteen. He looks at the two lines a long time, then draws a ruler through them, very neatly. "Clerical error," he says. Your name stays. Theirs are gone.

failure.text: He does not know the law and will not guess at it. He tells you to write to the company and wait for an answer, and the ferry leaves while you are still standing there holding his pen.

choices.label: Read the shoals and wade across at night
choices.intent: Rivers have marks too, for anyone who learned stones. Find the ford.
choices.risk: A river at night does not care what you can read.

success.text: You find the ford by the ripple over the sunken rocks, the way your father taught you to find a trail by the lichen on a cairn. Pip rides on your shoulders and Wenna holds your belt, and you come out on the far bank soaked to the chest, with nobody's name on any list.

failure.text: The ford is where you thought, but the current is stronger. You get all three of you across and lose the pack, one boot and most of the food. On the far bank Pip laughs at you for having one boot, and it helps more than it should.

choices.label: Pay something on account
choices.intent: Put food down, take a receipt, and cross as an honest debtor.
choices.risk: The company will count it as proof that you can pay more.

success.text: The clerk writes you a receipt in his careful hand and stamps it, and lets you cross. You fold it into the band of your hat. It is the first paper in your life that says you paid something instead of owing it, and you are surprised how much that matters.

cards.title: Small Cairns in the Dark
cards.flavor: At the crossroads someone has built little cairns at the mouth of each tunnel, no higher than your knee, in the old guides' language your father taught you on the Tablelands. Three stones and a flat one: water. Two and a split stone: wait here. And one you have seen only once in your life, a single stone set on its edge. It means followed. Down the left tunnel, faintly, a child is coughing.

choices.label: Follow them to the end
choices.intent: Find whoever built these and lead them out by a way only a Tablelands guide would know.
choices.risk: Whoever is being followed may take you for the one following.

success.text: At the end of the left tunnel are six quarry debtors and two of their children, out of food, out of lamp oil and out of cairns. They know you. One raises a pick. You set your lamp on the floor between you and say you can get them out, and then you do, by a seam your father showed you once that no catcher has ever walked.

failure.text: You find them, and they will not come. They have been led before, they say, and they look at you as if they know by whom. You leave them your lamp oil, half your food and the way out scratched on the wall, and you go on alone in the dark.

choices.label: Kick their cairns down behind you
choices.intent: Scatter every stone so nobody following them can read the way.
choices.risk: It is the very thing you swore off on the canyon ledge.

success.text: You kick them apart one by one, quietly, the way you did on the ledge above the forks, and the stones roll off into the dark. Whoever is following will lose the trail here. So will whoever comes after, looking for water. You stand a long while with grit on the toes of your boots again.

choices.label: Lay a false trail beside theirs
choices.intent: Leave their signs standing and build your own, pointing any catcher the long way round.
choices.risk: Anyone who reads stones as well as you will see your hand in it.

success.text: You build four cairns of your own down the right tunnel, in a hand a little older than theirs, pointing at water that is not there. Anyone following will spend a day learning that. On the last of their cairns you set one more stone, the sign for friend, and leave it.

failure.text: Halfway through you hear boots and a lamp coming from the way you came, and you have to leave the false trail unfinished. It points two ways at once. You never learn which way the catchers chose.

cards.title: No Cairns on the Glass
cards.flavor: The new black glass runs a mile wide across the road, still ticking as it cools, and nothing marks where the crust will hold. A line of families waits at its edge for somebody to go first. Wenna has seen the stones in your pack, the ones you have picked up at every ledge since the Tablelands without saying why. She asks if this is what they were for.

choices.label: Build cairns across the glass
choices.intent: Walk it slowly, test every step, and leave a stone marker at each sound place for everyone behind.
choices.risk: Slow on hot glass is its own kind of danger.

success.text: It takes the whole day. You go ahead with a staff, and at every place the crust rings true you build a cairn, three stones high, plain enough for anyone. By evening a line of them stands across the black glass, and the families are walking it without you.

failure.text: A crust gives under your back hoof halfway over, and you come out of it scorched to the hock. You finish the line limping. It is crooked in the middle where you could not see straight, but it holds, and the families cross.

choices.label: Guide them across for a day's food each
choices.intent: The old trade. You know the way and they do not.
choices.risk: You know exactly what you are charging for.

success.text: You take a day's food from each family and walk them over in a single line, never a wrong step. Pip eats well that night. Behind you there is not one stone on the glass, and the next line will wait at the edge for the next guide, and pay.

choices.label: Let Wenna build the cairns
choices.intent: Teach her the language stone by stone, while you test the crust well ahead of her.
choices.risk: She is eight, and she is proud, and she will want to go faster than you.

success.text: You test the crust and call back, and Wenna builds only where you call. Three stones, plain. At the far side she turns and looks at the line of them standing all the way across, and you watch her understand what a cairn is for. It is not what she saw you do on the ledge.

failure.text: She builds them too fast and too small, and twice you go back to do one over. It takes until dark. But they stand, and she sleeps that night with her hooves black from glass dust, smiling.

cards.title: A Big Back for Hire
cards.flavor: A company collector in a clean coat is clearing a homestead for debt, and he has two hired hands and not enough of them. He sees you on the road and brightens: a dollar a load to carry the family's goods out to the ditch, and nobody need raise a hand. A stoat widow stands in her doorway holding a skillet. Behind her skirts, three kits peer out at the biggest thing they have ever seen.

choices.label: Stand in the doorway beside her
choices.intent: Do not lift a hand. Just stand there, and fill the door.
choices.risk: If he sends for wardens, you will have to let them move you.

success.text: You say nothing. You stand in the doorway beside the widow with your arms folded, and you fill it from post to post. The collector looks at you a long while, does a sum in his head, and decides the debt can wait for harvest. The smallest kit pats your leg as he drives away.

failure.text: The collector sends for wardens. When they come you do not move and you do not raise a hand. It takes four of them most of an hour to shift you, and by then it is too dark to clear a house. The widow keeps it till Sunday.

choices.label: Carry their goods out, gently
choices.intent: Take the dollar a load, and see that nothing is thrown or broken.
choices.risk: The kits will remember who carried their cradle to the ditch.

success.text: You take the dollar a load and carry it all out yourself so nothing gets thrown: the cradle, the clock, the jars wrapped in a quilt. You set them in the ditch in a neat row. The widow does not thank you. The kits stop looking at you at all.

choices.label: Plough the south field by moonlight
choices.intent: A sown field is a harvest, and a harvest pays a debt. Put the harness on your own shoulders.
choices.risk: The plough was made for a mule, and the mule is long dead.

success.text: You take the harness on your shoulders and turn the whole south field by moonlight, the widow walking behind with the seed bag. The collector comes back at noon to a sown field and a neighbor ready to buy the crop standing. He tears a page out of his book and leaves.

failure.text: You get half the field turned before your shoulders give out and you go down in the furrow. The widow brings you water. Half a field is half a harvest, and the collector takes the other half in goods.

choices.label: Pay what she owes
choices.intent: Put everything you carry on the collector's book.
choices.risk: It is all you have between here and the next town.

success.text: You empty your pack onto the collector's book: coin, bread, the good knife. He counts it twice and tears out the page. It is less than one night's purse in the rings. It is the first money you ever spent that felt clean in your hands.

cards.title: Your Face on the Old Bill
cards.flavor: Nailed behind the trader's counter, brown with years of lamp smoke, is a fight bill from the Black Verge: THE IRON SAINT, UNBEATEN, with a woodcut of you twice as wide as you are. A young hare, barely grown, has been staring at it all morning. When you duck in through the door he looks from the bill to you and back, and asks, shaking, if you will teach him to fight. There is a purse at the Verge, and his mother owes for water.

choices.label: Tell him what the rings are
choices.intent: All of it, without dressing it up. The iron, the crowd, the night they brought in a child.
choices.risk: Told badly, the truth sounds like glory.

success.text: You tell him everything, plainly: the purse that is always smaller than the bill, the iron that never comes out of your wrists, the night Madam Ferrule led a pangolin girl into the ring and called it a fair match. He listens to the end. Then he takes the bill down himself and feeds it to the stove.

failure.text: You try, but it comes out as stories, and the stories sound like glory even to you. He leaves for the Verge that night with a bundle on his back and your old ring name in his mouth.

choices.label: Teach him to fall and get up
choices.intent: The one thing worth learning in the rings: how to go down without breaking, and walk away.
choices.risk: Teaching him anything may send him to the Verge.

success.text: Out back of the post you teach him to fall: on the shoulder, roll, up, and away. He goes down a hundred times and gets up a hundred and one. By dark he is sore and laughing, and he says walking away is harder than it looks. You tell him that is the whole lesson.

failure.text: You teach him too hard, the way you were taught, and forget how small he is beside you. He goes home bruised and angry, and you sit on the step a long time looking at your hands.

choices.label: Pay his mother's water debt
choices.intent: Put two days' food on the counter against what she owes.
choices.risk: You will walk the next stretch hungry.

success.text: You set two days' food on the counter against the water debt. The trader marks it paid. The boy stares at you, then at the bill on the wall, then runs home without another word about the Verge.

choices.label: Sign the old bill for the trader
choices.intent: He offers a week's food for your mark on it. A curio sells better signed.
choices.risk: The boy is watching you sell your old name.

success.text: You put your mark under the woodcut, and the trader wraps you a week of food. The boy watches you do it. When you leave he is still standing in front of the bill, reading your mark as if it were a promise.

cards.title: The Lintel Over Adit Four
cards.flavor: The timber over the fourth adit cracks like a rifle shot as you pass, and dust pours out of the dark. Six miners are shouting somewhere inside. The foreman will not send anyone in after them; the company counts timber dearer than diggers. The miners' children have come running up the spoil heap and stand in a line at the rope, safe and frightened, watching you, because you are the only thing on the hill big enough.

choices.label: Hold the roof on your back
choices.intent: Get under the cracked lintel and hold it while they crawl out.
choices.risk: If your knees go, the hill comes down on you and them.

success.text: You set your back under the cracked lintel and your feet in the rubble, and you hold. Six miners crawl out under your arms one at a time, coughing grey. When the last is clear you let go, and the adit closes behind you with a sound like a door. The children at the rope cheer.

failure.text: You hold until your arms shake and your knees buckle, and five come out. You go back in for the sixth with stone coming down round you, and carry him out on your shoulders. You will feel that lintel in your back for a month.

choices.label: Shore it with the company's timber
choices.intent: The company's best beams are stacked twenty yards off. Carry them in, two at a time.
choices.risk: The foreman will dock somebody for every beam.

success.text: You carry the company's best beams from the stack, two at a time, past the shouting foreman, and wedge them under the lintel until the dust stops. Six miners walk out on their own feet. The foreman docks their pay for the timber, and the miners split the loss without a word.

failure.text: A beam slips as you wedge it and catches you across the shoulder. The prop holds anyway, crooked. The miners dig the rest of the way out themselves by dark, and one of them is limping.

choices.label: Wait with the children for the company crew
choices.intent: It is not your mine. The company has a crew and a pump for this.
choices.risk: The children are watching what the biggest one on the hill does.

success.text: You wait at the rope with the children. The company crew comes at dusk with a pump and fresh timber and digs all six out by midnight, grey with dust, one with a broken arm. The children go home with their fathers and do not look back at you.

cards.title: Madam Ferrule's Iron Ring
cards.flavor: Inside the fortified camp the soldiers have built a ring of iron stakes, and a mink in a brocade coat is taking bets at its gate. You know her before you know the ring: Madam Ferrule, who held your purses for eleven years and led the child into the ring the night you walked out. She sees you over the crowd and smiles as if you had only stepped out for air. "My Saint," she says. "There's a purse tonight that would feed your whole road." In the ring a starving deserter waits, shaking.

choices.label: Take the purse and fight
choices.intent: Step over the stakes. It would be quick. It would feed you for a month.
choices.risk: This is the one thing you swore.

success.text: You step over the stakes. The deserter goes down in the first minute, and the crowd's roar comes up through your feet the way it always did, and for that minute it feels like coming home. Ferrule counts the purse into your palm. It is a great deal of food. It is exactly what you swore.

choices.label: Step into the ring and sit down
choices.intent: Go in, sit in the middle of the iron, and do not get up.
choices.risk: A crowd that paid for a fight will take its money's worth somehow.

success.text: You step over the stakes and sit down cross-legged in the middle of the ring, and you do not get up. The deserter stares at you, then sits too. The crowd boos, then goes quiet, then goes away. Ferrule loses the night's take and does not smile at you again.

failure.text: You sit, and the crowd throws whatever it has. Soldiers drag the deserter out to the stockade for spoiling the night. You sit there in the mud and the jeering until the lamps go out, and nobody else fights in that ring tonight.

choices.label: Ask her what became of Nell
choices.intent: The pangolin girl. You walked out and left her standing in the iron. Ask.
choices.risk: Ferrule sells everything, answers included.

success.text: Ferrule's smile slips. The pangolin girl, she says, was sold on with a wagon of indentures bound for the last threshold the week after you left; nobody would bet on a child who only curled up. "Past the gate by now, Saint. Or at it." For the first time in years you have a direction.

failure.text: She laughs and says one bout buys one answer. You walk away without either. At the camp gate a soldier who overheard catches your sleeve and says a pangolin child went through with a wagon of indentures, east, toward the last threshold.

choices.label: Buy the deserter's place
choices.intent: Pay Ferrule his stake and his ration, and walk him out of the iron.
choices.risk: Ferrule will remember that you paid her.

success.text: You count your food into Ferrule's hand until she shrugs and opens the gate. The deserter walks out of the ring on legs like string. He eats half of what you have left, slowly, and does not ask why. You do not tell him.

choice.label: Sing what your people sing for the dead
choice.intent: Take off your hat and give her the song your country gives its dead.
choice.risk: The hollow may not want a stranger's song over one of their own.

success.text: You take off your hat and sing, low and plain, in a language nobody in the hollow knows. The miner stops pouring. When you finish he says she would have liked it, and that by your custom and theirs together she is covered now. He ties the pouch with half his salt still in it, and his children eat tonight.

failure.text: Your voice catches on the second line, the way it has not since you left home. The miner waits politely until you stop, then goes on pouring. You stand with your hat in your hands until the last of the salt runs out.

choice.label: Bare your head to the dead sentry
choice.intent: Take off your hat and kneel beside the body, as you would for your own dead.
choice.risk: Soldiers dicing over a corpse do not like being watched by a stranger.

success.text: You take off your hat and kneel beside the blanket without a word. The dice slow, then stop. One by one the soldiers take off their caps. The youngest lifts the boots from the pot, laces them onto the sister's feet himself, and nobody throws again that night.

choice.label: Stand surety with your own name
choice.intent: Offer the hunter your name and your word as bond for the runaways' debt.
choice.risk: Nobody here knows your name yet. This will be the first paper to carry it.

success.text: The hunter has never been offered a stranger's honor as bond and does not know what to do with it, so he takes it, and writes your name carefully on the back of the writ. The mother and son walk out of the crack owing a debt they can carry. It is the first time your name has been written down in this land.

failure.text: He laughs at a bond made of words and walks toward the crack. You stand in his road, hand nowhere near your hilt, until he stops; by the time he loses his temper the runaways are long gone. He leaves you a bruise to remember him by.

choice.label: Fit her from your own string
choice.intent: Kneel by the ditch and find her size among the boots round your neck.
choice.risk: It is the pair you were saving for the smallest of the barefoot line.

success.text: You kneel in the ditch, check her feet against your paw, and unlace the third pair on the string. They fit. She stares at you as if you did a magic trick. Behind you the dicing stops, and one of the soldiers lays the dead sentry's boots back at his feet under the blanket. Nobody argues.

choice.label: Show the children the gap in the rocks
choice.intent: Teach the raccoon kids where a hungry crew hides apples so no warden ever finds them.
choice.risk: If the wardens see you, they will learn the trick too.

success.text: While the grown-ups argue at the gate, you take the three kids round the back and show them a crack in the rocks above the orchard, dry and cool and too narrow for a warden's arm. By dark half the apples are in it. The basket goes back to the road full of windfalls, and the wardens are none the wiser.

failure.text: The younger warden sees you coming back down the rocks with apple juice on your paws and makes you empty your coat. He looks at your mask a long time before he lets you go.

choice.label: Whistle the crew's call
choice.intent: Two notes, low then high. If he ever rode with Hollis, he will know it.
choice.risk: If he ever rode against Hollis, he will know that too.

success.text: His ears come up at the second note. He rode with the crew one season, before the leg. You share the arch, and he tells you where Hollis camps now and which caravans she will not touch. In the morning he hands you the saddlebags to take back. "Tell her the coyote from the arch says hey."

failure.text: He does not know the call, or pretends not to. He keeps one eye on you all through the storm, with the saddlebags under his head, and neither of you sleeps. At dawn you go separate ways, both a little more tired.

choice.label: Let Bao carry your bowl to the end of the line
choice.intent: Put your bowl in his paws and point him at the family turning away.
choice.risk: Bao has never once given up a bowl. He may simply eat it.

success.text: You put the bowl in his paws and point. He looks at the porridge, then at the smallest child at the end of the line, and walks it over with enormous care, spilling only a little. The child takes it. Bao climbs back into your lap very pleased with himself, and you stay hungry until noon and do not mind at all.

choice.label: Lift Bao onto the counter
choice.intent: Set a hot, coughing toddler right in front of the trader and his customers.
choice.risk: Bao is liable to grab the jar.

success.text: You lift him onto the counter, flushed and limp and coughing, in front of every customer in the post. The trader's chalk hand stops. Somebody in the line clicks their tongue at him. He sells the mother her bark at the first price, and breaks off a second strip for Bao without being asked.

failure.text: Bao grabs the jar. It comes off the shelf and smashes, and the trader takes the cost of it out of your pack, every crust, while the mother slips out with a strip in the confusion. At least she got one.

choice.label: Ask for a loaf for Bao, with no oath
choice.intent: He is too little to swear on anything. Ask her to feed him anyway.
choice.risk: Rules in the hollow are kept on the stone, and the stone remembers.

success.text: The baker looks at Bao, who is looking at the loaves with his whole face, and laughs. Children don't swear on her stone, she says; it is bad luck for the stone. She gives him the smallest loaf with no oath at all, and you a heel with one. Your echo comes back in his voice, which is the strangest thing you have ever heard.

failure.text: She says a rule is a rule. You swear for both of you, and the echo comes back twice: once in your voice, and once, very small, in his. You carry both oaths out of the hollow along with the bread.

choice.label: Tell him about the water house lock
choice.intent: You shot the lock off the Dustwater water house once. Tell him how that went.
choice.risk: If he has seen your notice, he has a year of water standing in front of him.

success.text: You tell it straight: the lock, the night the whole town drank, the empty cistern a week later, the price on your head. He listens with his paw on the padlock. Then he chalks a line on the stones, two cups a household, unlocks the lid for the family, and asks you to stand witness. You do.

failure.text: He hears the word Dustwater and his eyes go to your patch. He calls nobody, but he does not unlock the lid either, and he keeps a rock in his fist until you are out of sight. The family is still waiting when you go.

choice.label: Ask if he ever drove for the water house
choice.intent: Coyote to coyote: the water house hires drifters like the two of you for its night wagons.
choice.risk: He may know who you are, and what you are worth.

success.text: He drove one season, he says, before the leg, and quit the way you did, without his pay. The wagons still run every new moon, by the Tablelands road to a gate past the canyons, and he tells you which ford they use. In the morning he leaves you the saddlebags. "For whoever you're going after," he says.

failure.text: He laughs until it hurts his leg, and says every coyote in the territory drove for somebody. He keeps the saddlebags under his head all night and one eye on yours. At dawn you go separate ways, cold and wet, and neither of you has said anything true.

choice.label: Carry it to the gate with your face showing
choice.intent: Haul the box to the Crossing Gate yourself, notice or no notice.
choice.risk: Every toll keeper on the river keeps a sheaf of wanted faces.

success.text: You haul it nine miles with your hat in your belt. The toll keeper counts every token twice, then takes a notice from his drawer and holds it up beside your face. He looks a long time. Then he feeds it to his stove. "A thief doesn't carry a box nine miles to give it back," he says, and writes nothing down.

choice.label: Show her Lark's notice
choice.intent: Unfold the notice from your hatband and let her see you were told kind things too.
choice.risk: Two mothers' hope is heavier than one.

success.text: You unfold the notice: a bent-eared boy, his name in your letters and again in his. She reads it slowly, then looks at the ribbon. "They said a farm in the east," she says. "What did they tell you?" "Spring." You sit on the well rim together till dark, and in the morning she walks with you as far as the refuge road, to ask her own questions.

failure.text: She looks at the notice and hands it back quickly, as if it might be catching. "Mine's on a farm," she says. "Mine's on a farm in the east." You leave her retying the ribbon, tighter, and you don't blame her.

choice.label: Go aboard and nurse them yourself
choice.intent: You know fever. The last one you nursed, you gave away to strangers.
choice.risk: Fever does not care who you are sorry for.

success.text: You row out with a cask and climb aboard and stay. Three days you sponge foreheads and pour water into cracked mouths and sing whatever comes, and on the fourth the yellow rag comes down. A kit aboard asks why you cried the whole first night. You tell her the truth: you were practicing for somebody else.

failure.text: You nurse them four days and lose the old pilot on the third, and the fever gets into you before the rag comes down. You come ashore thin and shaking. The rest of them come ashore too.

choice.label: Speak as a mother who lost one
choice.intent: Tell the crowd what grief does when you hand it a rope.
choice.risk: Half of them have lost more than you.

success.text: You climb onto the stockade rail and tell them about the spring you lifted your boy into a kind wagon, and about every night since, when you would have burned the world for him. Then you lay your scattergun at the foot of the rope. Nobody throws it. The commander sends the raider to dig the camp's wells instead, and his children to carry the water.

failure.text: They listen, and some of them weep, and they throw the rope anyway. You do not watch. You walk out of the camp with the scattergun on your back and your paws shaking so hard you could not have used it if you'd wanted to.

choice.label: Tell him how your well went dry
choice.intent: You have sat beside a padlocked well before. Tell him what it turned your band into.
choice.risk: A keeper's son with a padlock does not want a lesson from a raider.

success.text: You tell him plain. The dry well had a lid too, and a lock, and a keeper who sold by the cup until the cup cost more than anyone had. After that it was your band on the lid, with a rifle. He listens with his paw on the key. At dawn he opens the lid for the family with the dry cart, a cup a head, free, and keeps the key.

failure.text: He hears the word raider and nothing after it. He calls his father up from the house with a shotgun, and you back off down the lane with your paws open while the family with the dry cart watches you go.

choice.label: Tell the line what you did at the dry well
choice.intent: You once put a thirsty old porcupine out for drinking out of turn. Tell them how that ended.
choice.risk: Every family at the pool will know what you are.

success.text: You stand in front of the line and tell it: the dry well, the ration, the old porcupine who drank out of turn for his grandkits, and how you put him out into the heat on your own say-so. You never saw him again. The oath-keepers let go of the newcomer's arms one at a time. Nobody looks at you, but nobody moves away from you either.

failure.text: You get as far as the dry well and your voice will not do the rest. The oath-keepers wait, then put the newcomer out into the storm anyway. You go out after him with your coat and walk him to an overhang a mile on, and come back alone, wet to the skin.

choice.label: Empty the band's purse at her door
choice.intent: Put down everything the band carries, wherever it came from, for the family with three children.
choice.risk: Your own band will go through the wall with nothing, or not at all.

success.text: You set the band's whole purse on her step, every coin and every cup of flour, honest and otherwise, and you do not let yourself sort which is which. The smuggler counts it twice and nods at the family. Their three children go through the side door ahead of your own kits, and your crew stands watching with empty sacks, and not one of them complains.

choice.label: Tell him where the clapper went
choice.intent: You saw the Abbess carry it down to the cistern the year you were given to her.
choice.risk: Saying it out loud, here, makes it true.

success.text: "She cut it out herself," you tell the caretaker quietly, "so no alarm could ever ring. It's at the bottom of the cistern under the cloister." He stares at you, then up at the gap in the bell. That night someone drags the cistern with a grapnel, and in the morning there is a bright new scrape on the bronze, where a clapper has been tried for size.

choice.label: Stand over the crack like a sister
choice.intent: No bounty hunter on this frontier lays hands where a sister is praying. You know exactly how a sister stands.
choice.risk: If he asks what house you are from, you will have to answer.

success.text: You sit down on the rock in front of the crack, fold your paws, and pray at him, steadily, in the voice they taught you, until he is embarrassed to be standing there. He goes up the other fork. When he has gone the mother in the crack whispers thank you, Sister, and you do not correct her.

failure.text: "What house?" he asks, and you hesitate one breath too long. He looks past you into the crack. In the end he takes them both, and writes in his book that a runaway novice was seen on the canyon road, and you know who reads such books.

choice.label: Say every name you counted
choice.intent: You kept the convent's silence for years. You will not buy a road with more of it.
choice.risk: Some of the names are ones you could have saved.

success.text: "No," you tell her, and then you say the names: every child you counted in the dormitory, every bed stripped to the boards, and every time you kept quiet to keep yourself safe. All of it, out loud, at the gate. It takes a long time. The negotiator listens to the end. Then she steps aside, which you did not expect, and you go through with nothing left unsaid.

choice.label: Cut his poppy with your blessed water
choice.intent: Sugar and sleep are the con. The poppy is the harm. Water it down until only the con is left.
choice.risk: He will know a fellow trader's work when he tastes it.

success.text: You stand him a drink, and while he is boasting you pour off half of each bottle and top them up from your jars. The cutters sleep a little less and wake a little more, and nobody at the quarry is any the wiser. Next morning the other peddler tastes his stock and looks a long while at your bell. Then he laughs, and buys you breakfast.

failure.text: He catches you with your jar at his bottle and slaps your paw away. "Brother," he says, "we're in the same line of work," and shoves you down the quarry spoil. The cutters line up for full-strength poppy while you dust yourself off at the bottom.

choice.label: Ring them away from the gate
choice.intent: Stand on the road with your bell and do your patter backwards: the water is better further on.
choice.risk: The smiling sister can hear every word.

success.text: You plant yourself on the road outside the arch and ring your bell at every family coming in, and tell them the water here is fouled and blessed two days on, and anyhow the sisters don't like children underfoot. Half of them believe you. They walk past the open gate in the dusk, and the smiling sister with the lantern watches them go.

failure.text: The smiling sister comes out with her lantern and asks you, gently, to move along; your water has made folk ill, she says. The families look at your jars and believe her. They go in, every one, and the gate stays open behind them.

choice.label: Trade the trader a blessed jar for the bark
choice.intent: Every trader had a mother who swore by something. Find his.
choice.risk: Some traders have heard of you.

success.text: You ring your bell on his counter and tell him the jar was blessed at a shrine his mother would have known, and watch his face for the moment it softens. It does. He takes the jar for a strip of bark, and the mother runs home with it. He keeps your jar on the high shelf beside the empty glass, and you hope he never opens it.

failure.text: "Blessed water," the trader says. "You're the hare from the south road." He has a cousin you sold to. He keeps the jar, keeps the bark, and keeps one paw on his cudgel until you are out the door. The mother is still at the counter, counting her coins.

choice.label: Give the jar your true name
choice.intent: Nobody has called you by it in forty years. Let it buy the old man both of his.
choice.risk: After this, you will only ever be Old Ash, even to yourself.

success.text: You lean to the jar and say the name your mother called you in the deep cave. Afterward there is a smooth place where it used to be. The witch on the barrel looks up sharply; she knows what a Storm Crow's own name is worth. She gives the old man two blankets, and he keeps his brother and his daughter both.

choice.label: Read the way off the brass crow
choice.intent: The token is coven brass. Whoever carried it knew the way, and brass remembers.
choice.risk: Coven brass remembers its debts, too.

success.text: You hold the disc to your eye and look. The tunnels open in your head the way the guide walked them, every turn, down to the chalk mark he left at the split. You lead the family through by noon, and on the far side you give the father his disc back. "Sell it to a crow," you tell him. "Never to a guide."

failure.text: The brass shows you the guide's last walk instead of his road: the tremor, the dark. You lead them the long way round, by the path you watched him fail to take, and it costs a day of food. They come out alive.

choice.label: Look through the charcoal
choice.intent: A drawing remembers the face that sat for it. Hold it to your eye and see who that was.
choice.risk: Wardens do not like witches reading their papers.

success.text: You ask to admire the portrait and hold it to your eye. The face that sat for it wore a warden's grey coat. You tell the warden, quietly, which of his own men it was and where that man hid his coat. He goes red to the ears, lets the young man go, and sends two wardens back down the line.

failure.text: The warden snatches the portrait back before the sight settles, and looks a long while at the ash on your feathers. He draws you himself, badly, and puts you on top of the sheaf. The young man is still arguing when you leave.

choice.label: Buy his writ and mark it served
choice.intent: A served writ cannot be served twice. Every honest hunter knows it.
choice.risk: It will cost you what the reward is worth to him.

success.text: He knows you by reputation and takes your offer for the paper, a little ashamed of how fast. You write served across it in your square hand, with the date, and sign it. No hunter on any road can carry it now. When he is gone round the bend, you hand it into the crack in the canyon wall.

choice.label: Ask the trader to show you the writ
choice.intent: No paper, no prisoner. It was the first rule you ever learned.
choice.risk: The trader may not like being taught the law by a stranger.

success.text: There is no writ, only a warden's say-so and a promise of flour. You tell the trader, loud enough for his customers, that holding a boy with no paper is kidnapping, and that you would be bound to bring him in for it. He lets go of the boy's collar very fast. The boy is in the reeds by dusk.

failure.text: The trader waves a scrap with a warden's scrawl on it and calls it paper. It is not, but it is enough for him and his customers. You stay till dusk anyway and walk the boy to the edge of the reeds yourself, and the trader tells everyone who comes in that you robbed him.

choice.label: Show him your writ book
choice.intent: Show him where the names from tally books like his end up: in books like yours.
choice.risk: It is a record of every name you ever served.

success.text: You open your book on his knee and turn the pages slowly: names, dates, prices, and which county paid. Some of them came off surveyors' lists. He reads a long while.
