Then he closes his tally book, hands out his grain by the head without writing anyone down, and climbs back out of the dark.

failure.text: He reads your book with professional interest and asks which counties pay best. You take it back too late. When you leave the crossroads he is still writing names, and a few of them are names he learned from you.

choice.label: Press your old seal into the tin
choice.intent: You still carry the water house seal ring. Make the can lid good.
choice.risk: Everyone in the post will know whose mark it is, and whose face.

success.text: You take off the seal ring you meant to throw in the river and press it hard into the can lid. The clerk looks at the mark, then at you, and fills the boy's jug to the brim without a word. The whole post has gone quiet. They know the ring. They know the face. You put the ring away, and do not throw it out yet.

choice.label: Tell him how it starts
choice.intent: You began with a lock exactly like this one. Tell him where it ended.
choice.risk: He may not want a baron's advice, even a fallen one.

success.text: You tell him: first a lock, then a price, then a ledger, then a drought, and then a mission with a spring and terms you could not refuse. It took you nine years. He listens with his paw on the padlock. When you finish he unlocks it, hangs the key on a nail where anyone can reach it, and chalks a ration line on the stones.

failure.text: He hears you out and says you would know, and that he is not you. He keeps the key. But he pours the family two cups without asking anything for them, and watches you while he does it, as if to prove something.

choice.label: Name the trick you used yourself
choice.intent: You weighed water short for years. You know exactly where this scale lies.
choice.risk: Saying how you know will cost you more than the sack.

success.text: You tap the stop under the left pan, where a filed notch lets it ride a quarter low, the same notch you once had cut in the water house scale. You tell the line how you know. The storekeeper looks at you, then at her own name on the debt board, and turns the pan over so everyone can see. The laborer's wife gets her quarter.

failure.text: You start to explain the notch, and the company man at the door asks how a stranger knows so much about short weight. The whole line turns to look at you. You leave before the question gets an answer, and the sack is still light.

choice.label: Tell him you kicked down cairns once
choice.intent: You know why a hungry man moves a marker. Tell him what it cost you afterwards.
choice.risk: He did not ask a stranger for a confession.

success.text: You tell him about the five cairns on the ledge, and your husband's debt, and the family that took the wrong fork because of you. He leans on the post a long time. Then he and his children pull the four posts and set them back on the true line, and he walks over to knock on the orchard family's door himself, about the seep.

failure.text: He hears you out and says your sin is not his, and he may be right. He tamps the last post down hard. You help his children carry their buckets, because they are small and it is a long way, and you say nothing more.

choice.label: Tell the room what a bought debt does
choice.intent: You were the widow by the door once. Say what happens to her after the gavel.
choice.risk: The land agent is not the kind who forgets a face.

success.text: You tell the room plainly: the debt passes, the interest grows, the children's names go up on a board, and the widow kicks down whatever she has to. Nobody bids after that, not even the agent, who examines his gloves. The trader sells the sheet to the widow herself for the price of a cup, and she burns it in the stove.

failure.text: The room hears you, and the agent bids anyway, a little higher, to show he can. The gavel comes down. On her way out the widow stops beside you and asks how long it took you to pay yours. You do not tell her that it is not paid.

choice.label: Tell him what five years at the quarry costs
choice.intent: Your husband signed a paper like that one. Tell the drifter what it bought him.
choice.risk: The recruiter makes his living on boys who do not know.

success.text: You tell him about Corran: the first year's pay gone on boots and company lamp oil, the second on interest, the cough that came in the fourth. You do not tell him about the fifth. The drifter looks at the paper with his mark on it, then takes it up and puts it in the fire before the recruiter can reach it. Nobody at that fire stops him.

failure.text: He listens, and he is frightened, but he is more frightened of the recruiter, who has two friends at the fire. He leaves with them at dawn. He takes your words with him, at least. Maybe they will be some use to him in the third year.

choice.label: Carry the mule in
choice.intent: It will not walk into the dark. It does not have to walk.
choice.risk: A mule is heavy and kicks, and the hail is coming down hard.

success.text: You crouch, get your arms under its chest and belly, and lift. The mule is so astonished it forgets to kick. You carry it down into the cave with the flour still on its back, and the packer walks beside you with his mouth open. Below, the sheltering families laugh for the first time in a week.

failure.text: It kicks you twice before you get it off the ground, and the second one lands. You carry it down anyway, limping, with the flour on its back and the packer apologizing the whole way.

choice.label: Offer them five backs in one
choice.intent: The sergeant wants a number of backs. Yours is worth five, and he can see it.
choice.risk: Somebody in the gang may know your face from the rings.

success.text: The sergeant walks round you twice, counts you as five, and cuts the brother loose. You haul spear shafts to the camp until dark. One of the gang knows you. "The Iron Saint," he says, "pulling a cart." You do not answer, and he does not say it again.

failure.text: The sergeant counts you as three, not five, and argues the rest all afternoon. You haul until morning before he cuts the brother loose. The girl is asleep against the milestone when you get back.

choice.label: Stake your back, not your fists
choice.intent: The recruiter knows your face and wants you to fight his bruiser for the paper. Offer him a season of hauling instead.
choice.risk: A season is a long time to carry somebody else's stone.

success.text: The recruiter weighs a drifter's five years against one season of you, and does the sum out loud. He tears the drifter's paper and writes yours. The drifter burns the pieces, slowly. Come thaw, the quarry will have the strongest back it ever bought, and not one blow struck for it.

failure.text: He laughs. He wants the fight, not the labor; a fight sells tickets. You will not fight. You leave the paper lying by the fire and the drifter looking at you as if you had promised him something.
